AI Tokenomics FinOps

Published as-is under MIT-0; this is not official AWS documentation. Prices and features change, so check the linked AWS pages before relying on a figure. To suggest a correction, use the Suggest a change link under any lever, or open an issue on GitHub.

Generative AI is billed by the token, so cost follows usage directly and rises as adoption spreads, often before anyone notices. Agentic workloads raise the stakes, because a single task can trigger many model calls. This runbook sets out the decisions that move the bill, for two kinds of team: those that adopt an AI coding assistant and tune how it is used, and those that build and operate an agent of their own. Start with the levers below, then work the track that is yours.

What you can change to optimise the cost

A lever is one change you can make to spend less. This runbook holds 35 of them. Each one either lowers the price of a model call or cuts how many tokens that call spends.

The grid below ranks the levers this runbook has scored, cheapest effort first, so you can see which ones pay off before you fund any engineering work. The list under it names all 35, with what each one saves, grouped by the team that owns the decision.

Both views above are built in the browser, so without JavaScript they do not appear. Every lever is still in this document: the lever progress board carries the full lever index, and Top levers by effort-to-savings carries the ranking.

Which track should I choose?

Choose Track 1 if your team wants to optimise the cost of using AI coding assistants such as Claude Code or Codex.

Choose Track 2 if your team builds an application that lets a model plan, use tools and take actions, and your team owns the cost of each model call.

Track 1 - AI Coding Assistant

Your organisation adopts an AI coding assistant and tunes how its teams use it.

Cost reasoning in this track uses the api-usage-based billing pricing model: you pay for input and output tokens per inference invocation.

Each lever is judged by what it does to token volume or token price. Seat and credit subscription plans change the currency, not the levers. On those plans, practices described in this article stretch usage allowances and credits instead of saving dollars.

    Model Inference

    Know how your coding agent is metered

    Challenge and why it costs

    Challenge. Coding agents are not all metered the same way. Some count tokens and requests against a monthly allowance, some count them against a rolling time window, and some draw down a monthly pool of credits. Each of those meters empties differently, so each one needs something different watched.

    Why it costs. A meter nobody is watching runs out mid-task. Depending on the plan the work then stops, queues, or continues as paid overage. So the cost of ignoring the meter is either lost developer time or a bill nobody approved.

    Assessment Answer each question for your workload, then open the guidance where you have a gap.
    Q1Do you know how your AI coding agent meters usage?
    How to close this gap best practice

    Best practice. Confirm which meter you are on before you build any monitoring, because the meter decides what there is to monitor. Pay-as-you-go platforms meter tokens and requests per unit time. Seat subscriptions usually meter a rolling time window. Credit plans meter a monthly pool.

    Q2Do you know what happens when the quota runs out: a hard stop, a queue, or paid overage?
    How to close this gap best practice

    Best practice. Confirm what happens at the limit before you reach it. Name one approver for paid overage or a budget increase, and define the response time.

    Q3Do you monitor that meter and alert before it empties?
    How to close this gap best practice

    Best practice. Alert on the metric you identified as your meter in the previous section, not a different one. Set the threshold so the headroom left when it fires covers the time it takes to get a budget increase approved. The slower that approval takes, the earlier the alert needs to fire.

    What it saves: Enabler — turns a quota limit into a decision you see coming. It saves nothing directly on the bill, but it keeps that limit from becoming a paid-capacity call made under pressure.

    Right-size the model to the task shared

    Challenge and why it costs

    Challenge. Each assistant offers models with different token prices and capabilities. Moving a routine task to a suitable lower-cost model can reduce spend without lowering task success.

    Assessment Answer each question for your workload, then open the guidance where you have a gap.
    Q1Do you set version-controlled model defaults centrally for the fleet?
    How to close this gap best practice

    Best practice. Treat the default as a platform decision. Distribute version-controlled configuration with a balanced session model and an efficient background model.

    If the fleet routes through an AI gateway, keep the tiering policy there. LiteLLM can classify each request into a configured complexity tier (LiteLLM, Auto routing [87]).

    Product controls differ. Claude Code's opusplan mode uses Opus for planning and Sonnet for execution instead of separating session and background defaults (Claude Code, Model configuration [88]).

    For Codex, choose the model and reasoning effort from task difficulty, then test the workflow (OpenAI Codex best practices [98]). This runbook uses the configured model as its starting point and changes it only when task evidence justifies the trade-off. Pair model choice with Match reasoning effort to task complexity.

    If Codex uses Amazon Bedrock, Bedrock is the inference, billing, quota, and AWS support boundary. OpenAI supports the local client and its configuration (OpenAI Codex on Amazon Bedrock [103]).

    Q2For each subagent, do you select its model and reasoning effort for the delegated task?
    How to close this gap best practice

    Codex subagents consume more tokens than comparable single-agent runs. Choose each subagent's model and reasoning effort deliberately, based on its task (OpenAI Codex subagents [100]).

    Claude Code's documented multi-agent example uses about 7x the tokens of a standard session, so keep teams small (Claude Code, Manage costs effectively [60], as of July 2026).

    A summarisation or mechanical subtask may suit a lower-cost model. If the subagent does difficult reasoning while the parent coordinates, assign capability accordingly.

    Define the split in Plan before executing complex work, then set effort through Match reasoning effort to task complexity.

    Q3Does your fleet default to low-to-moderate reasoning effort for routine, well-specified work, with deep reasoning switched on only by exception rather than left on by default?
    How to close this gap best practice

    Best practice. Deep reasoning adds output tokens, so using it for a one-line change costs more without improving the answer.

    Treat effort like the model tier. Ship a low-to-moderate fleet default in the same version-controlled configuration as the model defaults (Manage coding agent configurations).

    Codex guidance says to choose reasoning effort from task difficulty and test the workflow (OpenAI Codex best practices [98]). This runbook sets a low-to-moderate fleet default, then raises effort only when work needs deeper analysis. Set subagent effort separately when its task differs from the parent (OpenAI Codex subagents [100]).

    Use deeper reasoning for architecture decisions, subtle concurrency bugs, and long-horizon refactors. This question sets the fleet default. Match reasoning effort to task complexity covers the developer decision. Lower effort reports 50 to 70 per cent savings on straightforward tasks. Benchmark that on your own workload before quoting it.

    Q4Do you manage your fleet's model default as a lifecycle, not a one-time choice: trialling new models with a small group before they become the default, and auditing your pinned configuration against the provider's retirement schedule?
    How to close this gap best practice

    Best practice. A model default set once and never revisited decays from both ends: newer, cheaper models arrive while the one you standardised on drifts toward the vendor's own retirement date. Own both ends of that cycle.

    Evaluating in. Trial a new model with a small group before it becomes the fleet default, measuring quality, token counts, and cost per task on your own workloads rather than published benchmarks. Draw that group from teams who'll use it daily — they're the ones who'll notice reduced hand-holding or a broken workflow. Use the same experiment design as Measure cost per successful task, not cost per call: a comparable unchanged group, over real delivery work.

    Retiring out. Managed products handle retirement for you; a self-managed fleet doesn't — its pinned model settings and environment variables age into Legacy because nobody rechecks them (Claude Code, Environment variables reference [53]). Audit those pinned IDs against the lifecycle source for whichever plane bills you (Bedrock model-lifecycle guidance [16]; Anthropic, Model deprecations [62]), checking both if the fleet uses both — their schedules run independently. Schedule a Legacy or Deprecated model's migration ahead of its date rather than deferring it; full mechanics are in Track 2 (Audit for Legacy / extended-access models).

    Announcing the change. A default that changes silently reads to developers as the assistant getting worse. Share the evaluation's outcome through the same channels that carry the rest of the fleet's guidance (Developer education), so the reasoning travels with the setting.

    What it saves: The largest per-call multiplier a fleet holds is the frontier-to-mid-tier price spread. Central defaults apply it to every session, instead of only the sessions where somebody remembered to switch.

    Right-size the subscription plan

    Assessment Answer each question for your workload, then open the guidance where you have a gap.
    Q1Do you audit who actually uses what, and remove or downgrade inactive seats?
    How to close this gap best practice

    Coding assistants carry a per-seat licence cost that token-billed agentic work does not. That makes two actions here rather than one: remove or downgrade the seats nobody is using, and match the tier for the people who are (the next question). Audit who is actually active, then reassign or remove the rest (Claude, Purchase and manage seats on Team plans [89]). It also makes right-sizing the subscription plan Track 1's defining non-token lever: it is the one saving that does not depend on changing how anybody works.

    Q2Have you reserved Premium seats for members whose observed usage needs the higher limits, while keeping other members on Standard seats?
    How to close this gap best practice

    Match plan capacity to observed usage, then repeat the review before renewal. On Claude Team, Standard seats include Claude Code and base usage limits, while Premium seats add higher usage limits. Reserve Premium for members who need that extra capacity and keep other members on Standard (Claude, Purchase and manage seats on Team plans [89]). Use the Active members and assigned seats view with the per-user, per-model spend export to identify candidates, rather than assigning the higher tier by default (Claude, View usage analytics for Team and Enterprise plans [96]).

    Reassign seat types in Organization settings > Members. A Standard-to-Premium upgrade can take effect immediately and be prorated when extra Premium allocation is required. A Premium-to-Standard change takes effect at renewal and does not create a prorated refund. Removing a member frees that seat for reassignment, but reducing the bill requires reducing the plan's total seat allocation, which also takes effect at renewal (Claude, Purchase and manage seats on Team plans [89]).

    Do not apply this Team seat-tier rule to a usage-based Enterprise plan. That plan uses a shared consumption pool, so the relevant controls are organisation, group, and user spend limits, plus model defaults, model access, and effort limits (Claude Enterprise consumption guide [97]).

    What it saves: The organisation avoids paying for Premium capacity where Standard is sufficient and removes unused seat allocation at renewal. The saving depends on the organisation's contract and seat mix, so do not quote a multiplier without a current price source.

    Cost attribution and spending caps

    Challenge and why it costs

    Challenge. Without spending caps, saving money depends entirely on individual developers making the right call, task by task — and nobody reviews cost until a bill shocks someone. Most cost drivers are invisible mid-session, so when cost isn't something a developer is tracking, the default is the frontier model, not the right-sized one.

    A cap isn't there to punish developers or slow them down — it's there to make cost visible. That only works if two things come with it: a clear process for requesting more quota, and follow-up education on how to stay inside the budget next time (Developer education). Skip either one, and the cap becomes a silent throttle that costs productivity and trust instead of saving money.

    Assessment Answer each question for your workload, then open the guidance where you have a gap.
    Q1Do you understand your team's usage pattern and break down spend at user, team, and department level?
    How to close this gap best practice

    Best practice. Start from the path between the coding agent and its model. Use coding-agent telemetry for activity measures, and use the billing plane for charged inference.

    Use two complementary views. Coding Agent Insights works independently of the inference provider on its bearer-token path. Bedrock IAM principal allocation applies when Bedrock handles inference.

    • Coding agent telemetry with CloudWatch Coding Agent Insights. OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, and GitHub Copilot can emit OpenTelemetry data to CloudWatch. Coding Agent Insights records token consumption, per-turn latency, tool calls, API requests, and approvals. It slices these measures by organisation, department, team, cost centre, and user (Coding Agent Insights [74]). For Codex, follow the AWS setup guide so metrics populate the Codex dashboard tab (AWS OpenTelemetry setup for OpenAI Codex [104]).
    • Amazon Bedrock IAM principal cost allocation. Identifies which IAM users and roles invoke Amazon Bedrock, so per-user cost surfaces in the line_item_iam_principal column of Cost and Usage Reports 2.0. Session tags extend the same breakdown to team, department, and cost centre (Track Amazon Bedrock costs by caller identity with IAM-based cost allocation [75]).

    Where Codex uses Amazon Bedrock, Bedrock owns inference billing, quotas, and AWS service support. OpenAI remains the support boundary for the Codex client and its local configuration (OpenAI Codex on Amazon Bedrock [103]).

    If the assistant connects through a gateway:

    • Claude apps gateway. Fans out the same telemetry over OTLP/HTTP, and stamps each export with the developer's identity from your identity provider. CloudWatch dashboards then populate with user, team, and organisation attributes without you configuring every machine individually (Claude Code gateway telemetry [76]).
    • LiteLLM. Tracks spend per key, per user, and per team in the proxy itself. Attribution therefore comes from how you issue keys rather than from the backend's billing data, and the same layer carries the budget windows that turn attribution into a cap (LiteLLM, Budgets and rate limits [45], LiteLLM, Cut costs with Claude Code [73]).

    Other telemetry sources:

    • Seat plans. Per-user analytics and exportable spend reports usually ship with the plan (Claude Code analytics documentation [56]).
    • Credit-metered products. Per-user credit usage is usually provided in the admin views (Kiro pricing [58]).
    • Assistant-native OTel metrics. Where the assistant exports its own usage and cost metrics, you can point them at your existing observability stack instead of standing up a separate pipeline (Claude Code, Monitoring [54]).
    • Programmatic usage and cost reporting. A usage and cost API lets you pull the same figures into your own FinOps reporting on a schedule rather than reading them from a console (Claude Platform, Usage and Cost API [57]).

    Whichever tool you use, establish a baseline before you set a cap. Record a normal day and week per developer and team. This separates an expensive week from a busy one.

    CloudWatch does not know whether a coding task succeeded. Join its measures to a defined outcome through a stable task or workflow key, then calculate cost per successful task.

    Q2Do you have organisation-level spend caps and per-user limits enforced?
    How to close this gap best practice

    Best practice. Set organisation-level per-user limits with rolling reset windows and fail requests once a budget is crossed, so the stop happens on the request path rather than on the invoice. Amazon Bedrock has no native per-user spend limit, so a gateway is where this is enforced.

    • Claude apps gateway. Sets hard daily, weekly, and monthly caps per organisation, group, or user, and blocks requests at the cap (Claude apps gateway spend limits [72]; Introducing Claude apps gateway for AWS [42]).
    • LiteLLM. Enforces dollar budgets alongside tpm and rpm limits per key, user, and team, with short reset windows — stack a daily cap inside a monthly one so a burst is contained the same day (LiteLLM, Budgets and rate limits [45]). Its cost surface is wider than caps alone: fallback chains, prompt routing, prompt compression, and MCP auto-routing each reduce what a capped budget has to absorb in the first place (LiteLLM, Cut costs with Claude Code [73]). For a deployable reference architecture, AWS publishes a multi-provider generative AI gateway solution built on LiteLLM (Multi-provider generative AI gateway on AWS [77]).

    Where teams run the coding agent through their own AWS accounts rather than a shared gateway, add the account-native controls underneath. AWS Budgets can trigger a budget action that applies a restrictive policy or stops the target automatically once a threshold is crossed, so the account stops before the cap is breached rather than after the invoice arrives (Configuring budget actions [118]). Pair it with AWS Cost Anomaly Detection so an unexpected jump in spend alerts on its own, ahead of any fixed threshold, on each account that bills for inference (Getting started with AWS Cost Anomaly Detection [119]). The gateway caps enforce the per-user limit on the request path; these enforce the account-level ceiling and catch the anomaly the per-user cap cannot see.

    Q3Do you have a defined process for developers to request more quota when a task calls for it, a named approver, and a short turnaround?
    How to close this gap best practice

    Best practice. A usage limit's job is to make cost visible, not restrict productivity — that visibility is what makes developers more efficient and builds a cost-aware culture (FinOps Foundation, FinOps for AI [41]). Set it to cover most normal work, and pair it with an escalation path defined before anyone needs it: a way to request more, a named approver, and a short turnaround. Miss any of those three and the limit becomes a silent throttle that costs delivery time and trust instead of money.

    Where teams manage their own Bedrock quotas per account, wrap the standard escalation around the AWS-native request flow rather than inventing a parallel one. Service Quotas is the request path for a higher per-account limit, so the template, the named approver, and the turnaround target sit on top of it (Requesting a quota increase [120]). Point the criteria at the specific meters that gate the work, the per-model requests-per-minute and tokens-per-minute quotas for Amazon Bedrock, so a request names the quota it needs and by how much (Quotas for Amazon Bedrock [121]).

    Treat repeated requests as a signal to revisit the limit, not a rule to enforce harder, and pair it with developer education (Developer education).

    What it saves: Enabler — turns one shared invoice into spend you can see per user and per team. It saves nothing directly, but it's what lets a spending cap stop an overspend at the moment of the request instead of on next month's bill — and every other lever in this track needs that same visibility to work.

      Agent Harness

      Manage coding agent configurations

      Challenge and why it costs

      Challenge. Each release can add optional capabilities, including agent teams, dynamic workflows, long context windows, and scheduled tasks. Fleet defaults can enable them without a fresh review.

      Why it costs. These mechanisms can spawn agents, run background work, or retain more context. Without an inventory and measurement, developers cannot see which enabled capability drives usage.

      Assessment Answer each question for your workload, then open the guidance where you have a gap.
      Q1Do you maintain an evidence-backed inventory of optional features that materially increase token use?
      How to close this gap best practice

      Best practice. You cannot manage what you have not inventoried. Work with your internal AI champions (Developer education, Q4) to list the optional capabilities enabled across the fleet.

      Include agent teams, dynamic workflows, the 1M-token context window, scheduled tasks, and background work. Measure enabled use and completed outcomes before classifying a capability as expensive.

      For Codex, record model and effort defaults, subagent concurrency, instruction loading, and MCP catalogues. Its subagent guidance makes model and effort selection explicit (OpenAI Codex subagents [100]).

      Q2Have you disabled these token-hungry features centrally?
      How to close this gap best practice

      Best practice. Turn the inventory into version-controlled fleet configuration alongside model and reasoning-effort defaults. Use managed settings where the product provides them (Claude Code settings, available settings [80]; Claude Code, Permissions [81]). Deploy that configuration centrally so a setting cannot be overridden locally: Claude Code reads a managed settings file placed on each machine by the fleet, which is how a disabled feature or an allowlist stays disabled without trusting each developer to keep it that way (Deploy managed settings [122]).

      For Codex MCP servers, use enabled_tools and disabled_tools to narrow the catalogue. Set tools.<tool>.output_token_limit for tools whose responses can flood context (OpenAI Codex MCP configuration [101]).

      Record why each capability is enabled, then revisit the decision as products change. Coordinate the approved baseline through Manage organisational plugins.

      What it saves: Expensive optional features off by default, fleet-wide — agent teams, the 1M-token context window, scheduled tasks — instead of trusting each developer to notice they're moving the bill. The saving stays invisible until you inventory what's switched on.

      Manage organisational plugins shared

      Challenge and why it costs

      Challenge. When developers assemble their own toolset, every developer installs a different set of plugins, MCP servers, and skills. Efficiency gains found by one developer stay with one person. Unreviewed tooling spreads without anyone assessing its cost or data-handling behaviour.

      Why it costs. Configured tool catalogues and their metadata consume context, although implementations load them differently. Measure standing overhead and remove unused capability instead of assuming every definition is billed on every call.

      Assessment Answer each question for your workload, then open the guidance where you have a gap.
      Q1Do you ship a reviewed, approved baseline of MCP servers and skills at organisation, team, and project level, rather than leaving each developer to assemble their own?
      How to close this gap best practice

      Best practice. Curate the toolset in layers that match the work. An organisation baseline carries common tools, a team layer carries domain tools, and a repository layer carries project-specific tools. The servers in that baseline speak the Model Context Protocol, the open standard for how a coding agent connects to tools and data, so the reviewed set is expressed in one portable format rather than a per-product one (What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)? [123]).

      Ship deterministic governance in the same baseline. Lifecycle hooks run a fixed command on a defined event, so a shipped baseline can enforce a pre-commit lint, a security scan, or a session-start check without depending on each developer to wire it up. A third-party practitioner catalogue collects concrete, config-level hook examples across the event model that a baseline can standardise on; treat its figures as the author's own and validate them yourself before quoting (AY Automate, Claude Code hooks examples [124]).

      Start with one or two tools that remove a real manual loop. Measure their value and context cost, then expand only from evidence (OpenAI Codex best practices [98]).

      For Codex MCP servers, narrow each catalogue with enabled_tools and disabled_tools. Use per-tool output_token_limit when a response can dominate context (OpenAI Codex MCP configuration [101]).

      Put narrower tools one layer down or enable them only when the task needs them. Review standing overhead through Manage the session and its context actively, Q7.

      Q2Does third-party token-efficiency tooling go through your own security, supply-chain, and data-handling review?
      How to close this gap best practice

      Best practice. Community tooling cuts cost at points the assistant does not. For example:

      • RTK (Rust Token Killer) — CLI proxy that compresses shell command output before it reaches context (reports 60–90 per cent reductions on listings, reads, grep, git, tests). Bash tool only.
      • Ponytail — plugin that steers the agent to reuse existing code rather than write new code (reports ~54 per cent less code, ~20 per cent lower cost).
      • CodeGraph — builds a local semantic graph of the codebase and exposes it over MCP, cutting the tool calls needed to understand code. Savings scale with codebase size.

      None of these are products from AWS or from the AI coding agent vendors. Each one sits in the path of your source code and your prompts, so put it through your own security, supply-chain, data-handling, and telemetry review before you approve it. Then validate the saving on your own codebase, because the figures above are the projects' own reports.

      What it saves: A good tool set one team finds becomes the default for everyone. Keeping the same tools loaded fleet-wide keeps the prompt prefix identical across sessions, so caching keeps working, and it stops unreviewed tools from quietly working their way into what's loaded on every call.

      Run an open-weight model behind your coding-agent harness

      Challenge and why it costs

      Challenge. A coding agent is a model plus a harness. Most harnesses default to their vendor's frontier model, even though many can be pointed at a cheaper open-weight model through a compatible gateway.

      Why it costs. Every call then pays frontier per-token rates, including calls a cheaper model might solve. The saving exists only if cost per solved task holds, and only a benchmark on your own tasks can show that.

      Assessment Answer each question for your workload, then open the guidance where you have a gap.
      Q1Have you measured cost per solved task, not price per token, for each candidate open-weight model and harness pair on your own repositories and tasks?
      How to close this gap best practice

      Best practice. Benchmark each candidate model and harness pair on the measure set out in Compare models on cost per solved task, not price per token. Build the task suite from your own repositories, because a public benchmark rarely matches your codebase, languages or review standards.

      Hold the harness and inference setup fixed while you compare models, then hold the model fixed while you compare harnesses. Record the resolution rate, input and output tokens, cache hits and turn count for every task. Price each run at the Region and pricing tier you will actually use. Adopt the open-weight pair only when its cost per solved task beats the incumbent's on the same suite.

      Terminal-Bench 2.1 scores the model and the harness together, and the harness alone moves the result. Opus 4.6 scored 70.1 per cent on Claude Code and 63.8 per cent on Terminus 2. GPT-5.3-Codex scored 79.1 per cent on Codex CLI and 68.5 per cent on Terminus 2 (Terminal-Bench 2.1 [139]). Compare scores within version 2.1 only, because that release fixed 28 of its 89 tasks. These are the benchmark's own results, so validate the pattern on your own tasks before you rely on it.

      Use the public Terminal-Bench leaderboard to shortlist candidates. It ranks each model and agent pair by resolution rate, cost and tokens, and you can search it for the open-weight models you are considering (Terminal-Bench leaderboard [144]). Treat a leaderboard rank as a shortlist, then confirm the pair on your own tasks.

      A study by imec's aistack team ran two open-weight models across Claude Code, Codex and Pi on 64 tasks. Every combination resolved 44 to 53 per cent of the tasks, yet cost per resolved task ranged from $0.35 to $0.70 depending on the pair (aistack, Does your harness matter more than your model? [140]). Token efficiency drove that spread, because some pairs used far more input and output tokens for a similar result. The study used default settings and a small suite, so treat the figures as the authors' own and validate them on your workload.

      A controlled study ran 80 tasks from a private 256-task suite under each model's native harness and a neutral harness, and found no average advantage for the native harness (Harness or Model? Isolating the Harness Effect [141]). The neutral harness cost 1.2x to 1.6x as much per solved task, based on observed-usage estimates. The authors could not confirm the billed-cost ordering because usage records were missing, so treat the 1.2x to 1.6x range as directional. The study also found that 22 of 81 runs cancelled at the time limit had already produced a passing patch, so measure completion and correctness separately. These are the authors' results, so validate the ratios on your own suite before you quote them.

      Load-test the deployed endpoint for throughput and latency before you move developers onto it, using AWS's LLMPerf and LiteLLM guidance (Benchmarking customized models on Amazon Bedrock using LLMPerf and LiteLLM [138]). That test complements the task benchmark but does not measure task success.

      AWS runs its own evaluations of open-weight models across coding-agent harnesses. If you want help designing the benchmark or reading its results, ask your AWS account team to arrange a dedicated engagement with AWS specialists.

      Q2Have you reviewed the gateway, data-handling, and model-provenance path for the open-weight model, including whether it runs in your account on Amazon Bedrock or through a third-party API?
      How to close this gap best practice

      Best practice. Start with the managed open-weight models in Amazon Bedrock, which bill per token and need no infrastructure of your own. The launch list includes coding-oriented models such as Kimi K2.5, Qwen3 Coder Next and GLM 4.7 (Amazon Bedrock adds six open weights models [135]). Amazon Bedrock Runtime offers an OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions endpoint, and AWS recommends it for new applications. A harness's custom-provider setting can therefore point straight at a supported model, with no gateway in between (Amazon Bedrock, OpenAI Chat Completions API [145]). Check each model card to confirm the model supports that API on Bedrock Runtime, and check current Region availability before you choose, because the catalogue changes often.

      Put a governed gateway between the harness and the model. A customer-operated LiteLLM gateway on Amazon ECS (Codex with LiteLLM on Amazon ECS [136]) or Amazon EKS (LiteLLM gateway on Amazon EKS [137]) centralises model authentication, routing, budgets, rate limits and telemetry in your account. Set budgets and per-key limits in that same layer (LiteLLM, Budgets and rate limits [45]). The gateway holds model credentials and sees every prompt and code change, so review, patch and monitor it like any other in-path infrastructure.

      Running the model and the gateway in your own account keeps code and prompts inside your trust boundary. A third-party hosted API may log or retain them, so review residency, retention and training use for both the model provider and the gateway. Apply the same review you use in Manage organisational plugins, Q2.

      Open weight does not mean open source, and open source does not mean unrestricted commercial use. Verify the licence, the publisher and the integrity of the weights before you approve a model for developer use.

      Treat cyber capability as a threat-model input. NIST's Center for AI Standards and Innovation called GLM-5.3 "the most cyber-capable open-weight model released to date" (CAISI's assessment of Z.ai's GLM-5.3 cyber capabilities [142]). Anthropic's Frontier Red Team reported that the model's safeguards could be bypassed or removed with simple techniques (GLM-5.3 and the spread of advanced cyber capabilities [143]). Anthropic is a competing model vendor, and its finding concerns offensive capability and safeguards rather than coding quality. Weigh both findings in the security review of any open-weight model you consider.

      Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import is the in-account route when you need a model the managed catalogue does not offer (Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import [51]). If you then decide to own the inference, the Track 2 lever Self-host or distill when volume justifies it sizes the self-hosting economics, so this lever does not repeat them.

      Q3Have you confirmed that the chosen model's tool calling works cleanly through your gateway into the specific harness you run?
      How to close this gap best practice

      Best practice. Tool calling, also called function calling, is where a model swap usually breaks. Each harness expects its own tool-call format, and a gateway that translates between formats can drop or mangle calls.

      Compare the two harnesses on the same two questions: which provider runs inference, and whether a gateway sits in front of it. Both harnesses can call Amazon Bedrock directly as their provider, with no gateway in between. Claude Code calls Amazon Bedrock as its provider when you set CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK=1 (Claude Code on Amazon Bedrock [52]). Codex calls Amazon Bedrock Runtime as its provider when you set model_provider = "amazon-bedrock-runtime" (OpenAI Codex on Amazon Bedrock [103]).

      A gateway is optional and sits between the harness and the provider. Q2 covers the controls it adds. Claude Code can send its requests through a LiteLLM gateway when you point ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL at it (LiteLLM, Cut costs with Claude Code [73]). Codex can send its requests through a LiteLLM gateway on Amazon ECS, which then calls Amazon Bedrock as the provider (Codex with LiteLLM on Amazon ECS [136]).

      AWS's Codex and LiteLLM walkthrough validated streaming and function calling end to end through that gateway, but with an OpenAI model on Amazon Bedrock (Codex with LiteLLM on Amazon ECS [136]). No verified source shows the same parity for an open-weight model, so test every model, provider and harness combination yourself, both direct and through the gateway.

      Add tool-calling cases to the Q1 benchmark suite, including multi-step edits, file and shell tools, and parallel calls. Reject any pair that fails or loops on them, whatever its token price.

      What it saves: Frontier per-token rates on the work a cheaper open-weight model proves it can solve. Developers keep the harness they already use, and a governed gateway in your account carries the switch. The saving is real only after your own benchmark shows a lower cost per solved task, because a cheaper model that fails or loops can cost more.

        End User

        Developer education

        Challenge and why it costs

        Challenge. How well developers use an AI coding agent determines both its cost and its benefit. Caps and defaults bound spend, but they don't teach anyone how to work within it — a developer who doesn't understand a cap just works around it, and productivity suffers instead of cost.

        Why it costs. The tools change every few months. Developers who keep learning compound their advantage; developers who don't stay stuck on old habits. That gap in cost and effectiveness widens quietly across the whole fleet, on every task.

        Assessment Answer each question for your workload, then open the guidance where you have a gap.
        Q1Have you published an organisational AI coding agent guide, kept as a living document, that covers setup, the constraints in place and why they exist, session best practices, and how to request a higher limit?
        How to close this gap best practice

        Best practice. Give every developer the same starting point instead of leaving them to figure it out over months on their own. The anchor is a single organisational guide — kept as a living document, not a one-time launch, since the tools it describes change every few months.

        Cover four things: how to install and configure the assistant; what constraints exist and why; the prompting and session habits that keep cost down (session and context, reasoning effort); and the named process for requesting a higher limit (Cost attribution and spending caps) — that last part is what keeps a cap from landing as a silent throttle.

        Explain the reasoning, not just the rule: a constraint people understand gets followed, one that just shows up as a restriction gets routed around.

        Q2Does onboarding get the assistant installed and correctly configured on day one, with the organisation-level settings and skills, the team's own, and whatever the repository ships?
        How to close this gap best practice

        Best practice. A developer's first week sets habits that stick — and if that week runs on default configuration, they're paying the expensive default the whole time. Make day-one setup an explicit step that installs all three configuration layers: organisation settings and skills, the team's own, and whatever the repository ships. This question is simply whether those layers actually land on a new machine — you already define them in Manage organisational plugins and enforce them in Manage coding agent configurations.

        Verify it landed, don't just tell them to set it up: have the developer confirm the model default, reasoning-effort default, and tool set they actually ended up with. A setup step that silently failed looks identical to one that was never run.

        Q3Do developers learn the habits through pair and mob programming on real work, using existing external courses for the fundamentals instead of building your own training from scratch?
        How to close this gap best practice

        Best practice. Context management, effort matching, and good prompting are hard to teach as rules but obvious when you watch someone do them. Pair and mob programming on real tasks is how they spread — a developer sees a colleague reset context, plan before a multi-file change, or phrase a request that lands first time.

        Don't build the fundamentals yourself. Anthropic Academy has free self-paced courses with certificates, including Claude Code in Action, AI Fluency, and Model Context Protocol (Anthropic Academy [78]). AWS Skill Builder has generative AI learning plans, role-based courses, and hands-on labs, free with an optional paid tier (AWS Skill Builder [79]). Your AWS account team can also run a coding-agent workshop or architecture review at no cost. Spend your own effort only on what no external course covers: your codebase, your constraints, your tooling.

        Q4Do you sponsor internal AI champions and run a community of practice, so new practices and cost wins found by individuals spread across the organisation?
        How to close this gap best practice

        Best practice. New models and features ship faster than any platform team can document them — the developers using the tools daily find the new tricks first. A written guideline captures what was true when someone wrote it down; a community of practice captures what's true right now.

        Give internal AI champions real time to experiment, and expect them to share what they find — through internal sessions and a forum for trading usage patterns, configurations, and cost wins. Fund it properly; unfunded enthusiasm fades. Then feed what they find back into the actual artefacts: an update to the guide (Q1), a candidate for the curated baseline (Manage organisational plugins), or a new fleet default — not something that stays known only to one team. This is also how a changed default gets explained, since a default that changes silently just looks like the assistant getting worse.

        What it saves: Enabler — this is what makes every other Track 1 lever actually work. It saves nothing directly on the bill, but it's the difference between a cap developers understand as a signal and one they just experience as an obstacle to route around. (Qualitative: you'll see the gap it closes in your per-developer attribution data.)

        Manage the session and its context actively shared

        Challenge and why it costs

        Challenge. A coding agent re-sends its context on every message, so a long-lived session resends its whole accumulated history every turn. That makes stale or oversized context the largest source of silent waste in Track 1. Every irrelevant file, finished sub-task, and abandoned thread is re-billed on each turn for the rest of the session.

        Why it costs. Because the whole working set is re-billed every turn, an append-only session keeps paying for context the current task no longer needs, and the charge grows every turn. Wrong-direction detours are paid for twice: the tokens the detour spent, and the detour's residue re-sent on every turn after it.

        Assessment Answer each question for your workload, then open the guidance where you have a gap.
        Q1Do developers reset context between unrelated tasks, rather than waiting for automatic compaction?
        How to close this gap best practice

        Best practice. Run the assistant's clear command when you start a new task. Do not wait for auto-compaction. By the time it fires, the context is already full and you have paid for far more tokens than the task needed. The vendor's own worked comparison puts three tasks run in one session at 1.9x the tokens of the same three with a clear between them (Maximizing the value of your Claude Code sessions [90]).

        Name the session before you clear it. Clearing does not delete the old one, but the resume list gets hard to read once a day's worth have accumulated. A developer who fears losing the thread will keep working in one context instead, so renaming first removes that reason (Claude Code, Manage costs effectively [60]).

        Keep one chat per coherent outcome. In Codex CLI, use /new when the outcome changes and /compact when the same outcome still needs a long chat (Codex CLI developer commands [106]). Command availability varies by surface. The ChatGPT desktop app documents /compact, /plan, and /review separately (Codex desktop slash commands [102]).

        Q2Do you use rewind features to unwind a change the coding agent made?
        How to close this gap best practice

        If the agent goes down the wrong path, rewind to a checkpoint instead of carrying on. Otherwise the failed attempt stays in context and you pay for it again on every turn that follows.

        Rewinding is also the cheaper of the two ways to shed context. A rewind costs nothing, while compaction rewrites the conversation and loses the prompt cache with it, so the next turn re-prefills at full price (Maximizing the value of your Claude Code sessions [90]). Reach for rewind when you know which turn went wrong, and for compaction only when the whole history has to go.

        Q3When a session repeatedly reaches its context limit, do you identify the source before resetting it?
        How to close this gap best practice

        Best practice. Most assistants have a command that shows exactly what's filling your context — which tools and files used the tokens, plus cache misses and oversized files (Claude Code, Manage costs effectively [60]). Check that before you reset, so you fix the actual cause instead of hitting the same wall next session. If your assistant fires lifecycle hooks around compaction and session start, automate this check fleet-wide rather than relying on developers to remember (Claude Code, Hooks reference [63]).

        Run the same command in a fresh session too, before anyone has done any work. What it reports there is your standing overhead: the instruction files, tool definitions and connected servers every session pays for whether it uses them or not (Maximizing the value of your Claude Code sessions [90]). That number is the one Q6 and Q7 below act on, and it is invisible if you only ever look at a session that has already filled up.

        Q4Do developers point the agent at specific files by path rather than asking it to discover them through open-ended exploration?
        How to close this gap best practice

        Best practice. Precise reads keep the working set small from the start. Point the agent at specific files by path rather than asking it to go and find them: "read src/auth/login.ts and src/auth/session.ts" spends no tokens on exploration. That matters twice over, because every file an exploration pulls in is then re-billed on every turn that follows. The vendor documents this as the way to work in a monorepo or large codebase: give the agent the paths and the structure instead of letting it search (Set up Claude Code in a monorepo or large codebase [125]).

        Where the assistant supports an attach syntax, use it rather than naming the file in prose. Naming it still costs a read turn. Attaching it puts the contents in the prompt directly. The vendor's worked example runs one request three ways. Asking "the tests are failing" spends six turns searching before the fix even starts. Naming the file spends one. Attaching it with @ spends none (Maximizing the value of your Claude Code sessions [90]).

        Q5Do developers keep large command output out of the main session by filtering it or delegating bounded analysis?
        How to close this gap best practice

        Best practice. Large command output can pollute the main context and be re-sent on later turns. Stop unnecessary output before deciding whether to delegate it. The vendor's cookbook treats this as context engineering: clear a tool result once it has been used, compact when the history has served its purpose, and keep only what the current step needs in the window (Context engineering: memory, compaction, and tool clearing [126]).

        Use quiet flags such as --silent, -q, and -no-color. Filter to failures when a quiet flag would hide the answer. Put those defaults in the instruction file (Maximizing the value of your Claude Code sessions [90]).

        Codex subagents consume more tokens than comparable single-agent runs because each agent performs its own model and tool work. Use bounded parallelism only for independent, read-heavy exploration, tests, triage, log analysis, or summarisation. Avoid parallel writes by default (OpenAI Codex subagents [100]).

        Use delegation to isolate necessary noise, not as a default saving. Define the split in Plan before executing complex work, then measure net tokens and successful outcomes through Cost attribution and spending caps.

        Q6Do you keep your always-loaded instruction files small, pushing occasional workflows on-demand and pruning them periodically?
        How to close this gap best practice

        Best practice. Keep always-loaded instruction files limited to conventions, the directory map, and key commands. Move specialised workflows into on-demand skills or separate documents.

        Codex reads guidance from global scope, then from the project root down to the current working directory. Closer AGENTS.md or override files win. The combined project-document cap defaults to 32 KiB and is configurable (Codex custom instructions with AGENTS.md [99]).

        Keep shared guidance at the root and place narrow overrides close to the code they govern. This prevents broad instructions from carrying project-specific detail into every task.

        Claude Code documents a target below 200 lines for its always-loaded instruction file (Claude Code, Manage costs effectively [60], as of July 2026). Prune periodically because these files tend to grow.

        Q7Do developers review their configured MCP servers periodically and remove the ones no longer in use?
        How to close this gap best practice

        Best practice. Review configured MCP servers and remove those that no longer support a real workflow. Implementations load catalogues differently, so measure standing context rather than assuming a fixed overhead.

        Codex supports enabled_tools, disabled_tools, and per-tool output_token_limit controls (OpenAI Codex MCP configuration [101]). Start with one or two tools that remove a manual loop, then expand only from evidence (OpenAI Codex best practices [98]).

        The fleet-wide counterpart to this habit is Manage organisational plugins.

        Q8Do developers pick the model and the reasoning effort before the first prompt, rather than switching part-way through a session?
        How to close this gap best practice

        Best practice. Both settings sit in the cached prefix, so changing either one part-way through a session invalidates the cache. The whole conversation is then re-prefilled at the new model's price, and toggling fast mode does the same (Maximizing the value of your Claude Code sessions [90]). Decide both before the first prompt.

        Read this alongside Match reasoning effort to task complexity. That lever is right that effort should follow the task, and session start is where following it is cheap. Escalating once the conversation has grown means paying for the re-prefill on top of the deeper reasoning.

        The cache also expires on its own, after an hour on a subscription and five minutes on an API key (Claude Code, Manage costs effectively [60]). Coming back after that re-prefills at full price too, so compact before a long break rather than after it. Track 2 carries the read and write multipliers behind all of this (Place and verify cache checkpoints).

        What it saves: 20 to 40 per cent on long sessions from the documented context habits. Delegating noisy work protects the main thread but can increase total tokens, so count it only when measured cost per successful task improves (Measure cost per successful task).

        Match reasoning effort to task complexity

        Challenge and why it costs

        Challenge. Extended "thinking" is a token cost like any other, and applying maximum reasoning to a one-line rename is the cognitive equivalent of routing trivial work to a frontier model.

        Why it costs. Deep reasoning generates many extra output tokens, the most expensive kind, so spending it on routine work inflates cost with no quality gain.

        Assessment Answer each question for your workload, then open the guidance where you have a gap.
        Q1Do developers choose reasoning effort from task difficulty and validate it on representative workflows?
        How to close this gap best practice

        Best practice. Choose reasoning effort from task difficulty, then validate it on representative workflows. Use lower effort for routine, well-specified work and raise it only when deeper analysis improves results.

        Claude Code exposes effort through /effort, /model, or MAX_THINKING_TOKENS on models with a fixed thinking budget (Claude Code, Model configuration [88]).

        Codex guidance says to choose effort from task difficulty, then test what works for your workflow (OpenAI Codex best practices [98]). Set the fleet default in Right-size the model to the task, Q3.

        Q2Is deep reasoning escalated by exception, reserved for complex work?
        How to close this gap best practice

        Reserve deep reasoning for multi-step planning, architecture decisions, subtle concurrency bugs, and long-horizon refactors. Escalating by exception keeps the expensive setting where it earns its cost.

        For Codex subagents, select the model and model_reasoning_effort deliberately when the delegated task differs from the parent (OpenAI Codex subagents [100]).

        What it saves: 50 to 70 per cent on straightforward tasks, because deep reasoning spends extra output tokens, the most expensive kind, and routine work gains no quality from them.

        Plan before executing complex work

        Challenge and why it costs

        Challenge. Diving straight into edits on a non-trivial change risks discovering a wrong assumption only after the agent has generated, tested, and partially integrated the wrong solution.

        Why it costs. Late discovery of a wrong assumption causes avoidable generation, test, and integration work. A planning pass can expose the assumption before code is written. Measure the local difference instead of relying on a universal token benchmark.

        Assessment Answer each question for your workload, then open the guidance where you have a gap.
        Q1Is plan-then-execute the default way developers approach a non-trivial task?
        How to close this gap best practice

        Best practice. Use a read-only planning pass for multi-file changes and unfamiliar code. Codex Plan mode can inspect context and propose an approach before implementation starts (OpenAI Codex best practices [98]).

        Review the plan while assumptions are cheap to correct. If local evidence supports different model tiers for planning and implementation, apply Right-size the model to the task.

        Q2Does the plan define the tests, lint or type checks, review criteria, and stopping condition that prove the task is done?
        How to close this gap best practice

        Best practice. Structure the task as Goal, Context, Constraints, and Done when. Use Codex Plan mode before implementation (OpenAI Codex best practices [98]).

        Make Done when observable. Name the smallest relevant tests, lint or type checks, review criteria, and stopping condition. OpenAI recommends running relevant tests, lint or type checks, and a final review (OpenAI Codex best practices [98]). This runbook's decision rule is to run targeted checks first, then use /review before completion (Codex CLI developer commands [106]).

        Record the successful outcome so telemetry can be joined to it later. See Measure cost per successful task, not cost per call.

        What it saves: Avoided rework from assumptions caught before implementation. Measure the planning cost against generation, test, and integration work avoided on comparable tasks.

          Track 2 - Purpose-Built Agentic AI Application

          A purpose-built agentic AI application uses a model in a loop to plan, call tools and act toward a goal. Inference means one model call. The agent harness is the application code that supplies context, tools, memory and loop controls.

          You build and operate the agent — you own the architecture, the prompts, the model choice, the orchestration and the Bedrock call itself. Every lever here needs that ownership: how you route a request, where it runs, and how you stop one that runs away.
