            Model Inference

            Include in this assessment: Model Inference

            Untick a lever that does not apply to your workload. Its questions are hidden and left out of every count, summary and export; the choice is saved in this browser. Clicking a box in the figure above does the same.

            Know what you spend and what it buys

            Challenge and why it costs

            Challenge. An agentic workload does not make one model call per user task: it loops, re-sending accumulated context on every pass. Token cost therefore scales faster than adoption, and a pilot that looked cheap at ten users is expensive at a hundred, non-linearly. Without a way to decompose total spend into the terms that drive it, every anomaly becomes a billing dispute rather than an engineering investigation.

            Why it costs. Token counts measure usage, not value. No executive can act on "we used 3.2 billion tokens"; everyone can act on "cost per resolved ticket fell 18% while volume doubled" (FinOps Foundation, Unit Economics capability [91]). Without outcome-denominated metrics, you cannot tell whether a model swap, a prompt change, or an architecture decision made things better or worse. And without per-workload attribution, overspend cannot be traced to the team or application that caused it (AWS ML Blog, Track and allocate Bedrock cost [107]; WA Agentic AI Lens, AGENTCOST01 [39]).

            Assessment Answer each question for your workload, then open the guidance where you have a gap.
            Q1Do you know your total agent spend and how it is constructed?
            How to close this gap best practice

            The short answer. Write the equation down and measure every term: spend = users × sessions per user × turns per session × requests per turn × tokens per request × price per token. When the bill moves, name the term that moved it.

            Worked example

            Uber's cost equation in practice

            Uber decomposed their AI spend into exactly this equation (Uber Engineering, Running a Software Factory Efficiently at Uber Scale [109]). From February to August 2026, weekly active users across all agentic offerings grew 7x and weekly requests grew 9.4x, yet total spend stabilised because they optimised the middle terms (turns, tokens, price). Holding one model fixed, they measured a 34% drop in cost per 1,000 requests and a 52% drop in cost per session. The decomposition told them exactly where the savings came from: not from cutting usage, but from reducing waste in each term while letting adoption grow.

            Read more for the self-serve reader

            What is your cost equation? Total agentic spend is the product of several terms that multiply together: users × sessions per user × turns per session × requests per turn × tokens per request × price per token. Each term can be measured and improved independently. When the bill moves, the goal is to point at exactly which term moved it, with nothing left unexplained.

            Why this matters for agents. Agentic workloads amplify cost: one task becomes multiple tool-call rounds, and each round re-sends the full conversation so far. Cost per task grows roughly with the square of the number of rounds, not linearly. Without explicit caps on iterations, token budgets, or confidence thresholds, the invoice is often the first sign something is wrong (WA Agentic AI Lens, AGENTCOST01 [39]).

            Do you have the observability to gather this? Most of the signals you need already flow through standard AWS cost tooling and any OpenTelemetry-compatible telemetry pipeline. Confirm you can see: your monthly invoice broken down by service and tag (CUR 2.0), per-application token metrics from tagged Bedrock inference profiles (CloudWatch), gateway or API logs showing who called what and when, and per-request logs for spike investigation. If your agents run outside AWS, the same signals are available through OpenTelemetry exporters into CloudWatch or your existing observability stack (CUR 2.0 [108]; Bedrock invocation logging [47]).

            Break down each month's bill movement into four drivers: adoption (more users), engagement (more requests per user), input workload (more tokens per request), and output workload (more output tokens per request). This is how you answer "why did the bill go up" without guessing.

            Q2Do you track cost per successful task, and gate releases on it?
            How to close this gap best practice

            The short answer. Divide spend by what it bought: cost per successful task = total spend across all attempts / successful outcomes, and fail a release that raises it even when quality holds.

            Read more for the self-serve reader

            Define the unit of work. For each agent or use case, name the business outcome it delivers: a conversation handled, an invoice processed, a code review completed, an alert resolved. Then track cost per successful task = total spend across all attempts / successful outcomes. The denominator matters: if only 70% of attempts succeed, the effective cost per success is 1.43x the per-attempt figure. A falling success rate is a cost regression even when the per-call price has not changed (FinOps Foundation, Unit Economics [91]).

            Track outcomes alongside cost. For every managed agent, measure three things together: (1) outcome-denominated cost (cost per completed task, cost per review, cost per alert), (2) quality signal (error rate, accuracy, time-to-resolution), and (3) volume (tasks completed, reviews posted). This tells you whether each agent is getting cheaper per unit of value delivered, and whether quality holds when you swap models or change prompts.

            Gate releases on cost, not just quality. Track token-per-task in your test suite alongside accuracy for every change to prompts, tools, or models. Gate merges on the budget the same way you gate on accuracy. A prompt tweak or a model swap can quietly double per-task tokens, and nothing in the release process catches it until the invoice unless cost is in the gate (WA Agentic AI Lens, AGENTCOST01 [39]).

            The maturity path. Start with cost per token (you can compute it from your invoice today). Mature toward cost per outcome by wiring your release pipeline to record both accuracy and token-per-task. The FinOps Foundation frames this as the standard progression for AI workloads (FinOps for AI Working Group [41]).

            Q3Is every dollar attributed to the team or workload that caused it?
            How to close this gap best practice

            The short answer. Attribute in layers, strongest first: the team’s own account, then a tagged application inference profile per application or tenant, then cost allocation tags, then per-user tracking. Call the model through the profile ARN, never a raw model ID.

            Read more for the self-serve reader

            Layer your attribution, strongest first. (1) Account boundaries: keep the AI model calls in the team's own AWS account so the bill lands directly on the team that caused it. (2) Application inference profiles: tag one profile per application or tenant, and always call the model through the profile ARN rather than a raw model ID. The profile's CloudWatch metrics give you near-real-time token counts per workload. (3) Cost allocation tags: at minimum business_unit, application, environment, and cost_centre, activated in the billing account before launch. (4) Per-user tracking: use IAM principal cost allocation to see per-person spend in your invoice (AWS CFM Blog, IAM-based cost allocation [75]; Bedrock inference profiles [18]).

            Allocate shared platform costs. Some costs (gateway, policy engine, monitoring) are shared across teams. Split them using logged per-team usage shares for traffic-driven costs, and an even or tiered split for fixed costs. Document the formula and review it annually. Start with a transparency report ("showback") for the first quarter while the numbers stabilise, then switch to chargeback once teams trust the numbers (AWS Tagging Best Practices [110]).

            Make the numbers visible in time to act. Attribution is useless if nobody sees it until month-end. Set budget alerts per team account (monthly + daily, filtered to your AI service) with automatic restrictions at 100%. Add anomaly detection scoped per account. Best practice is a live cost indicator visible to the developer during their session, with automated alerts at 50%, 80%, and 100% of expected spend (AWS CFM Blog, Budget Actions [111]).

            What it saves: Visibility first. It saves nothing directly on the bill, but every other lever in this layer needs this decomposition to tell you whether it worked.

            Route to the right model shared

            Challenge and why it costs

            Challenge. The per-token spread between a frontier model and a light one spans one to two orders of magnitude, yet most teams default every call to the frontier. Meanwhile, pinned model IDs age into Legacy pricing without anyone re-reading them.

            Why it costs. Without deliberate per-step routing, the entire workload pays frontier prices. Without lifecycle auditing, Legacy models silently move to a higher price tier (Amazon Bedrock pricing [1]; Bedrock model-lifecycle guidance [16]).

            Assessment Answer each question for your workload, then open the guidance where you have a gap.
            Q1Does each request go to the cheapest model that meets your quality bar?
            How to close this gap best practice

            The short answer. Send each step to the cheapest model that clears your quality bar, judged by cost per solved task: blended cost = f × cheap model cost + (1 − f) × frontier model cost, where f is the fraction of requests the cheaper model can serve.

            Worked cost example

            Tiered routing with GPT-5.6 Sol and Luna

            The blended monthly cost is blended_cost = f × cheap_model_cost + (1 − f) × frontier_model_cost, where f is the fraction of prompts the cheaper model can serve at acceptable quality. Savings versus a frontier-only baseline are f × (1 − cheap_model_cost / frontier_model_cost). This example uses one million requests per month, averaging 2,000 input and 500 output tokens each, with 60% routed to Luna.

            ItemGPT-5.6 SolGPT-5.6 Luna
            Input price (per 1M tokens)$4.40$0.22
            Output price (per 1M tokens)$22.00$1.32
            Cost per request (2,000 in / 500 out)$0.01980$0.00110
            • Sol-only baseline: 1,000,000 × $0.01980 = $19,800 / month
            • Tiered (60% Luna / 40% Sol): (600,000 × $0.00110) + (400,000 × $0.01980) = $660 + $7,920 = $8,580 / month
            • Savings: roughly 57%
            • IPR surcharge avoided: one million requests routed through Intelligent Prompt Routing adds $1 per 1,000 requests, or about $1,000 / month, on top of model-token cost (Amazon Bedrock pricing [1]).

            The arithmetic is illustrative, not a quality recommendation. Recompute it with the live prices, context band, Region, and models your evaluation set selects.

            Read more for the self-serve reader

            Task-tier routing. Route each prompt to the cheapest model that clears your quality bar, judging tiers by cost per solved task, not price per token. AWS Prescriptive Guidance recommends this cascade as a core cost pattern (APG, Agentic AI cost optimisation [7]; APG, Selecting the right model on Amazon Bedrock [46]). The Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens calls it out as a model-cost best practice (AGENTCOST02 [4]).

            Where to run the routing. Options fall into two camps:

            • Managed AI gateways. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway [32] routes across Bedrock, OpenAI, Anthropic, and other OpenAI-compatible providers. LiteLLM router [48] and Portkey [49] add multi-model routing with budget and policy controls.
            • Open-source semantic routers. vLLM Semantic Router [112] classifies each request by intent and routes to the model tier that fits; NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard [113] orchestrates model selection and fallback across a fleet of self-hosted models.

            Real-world implementation. Spotify's Portal plugin applies task-based routing to Claude Code by classifying each call as I/O or reasoning. Pre-tool-use hooks intercept file reads above a configurable line threshold and redirect them to a cheaper worker model (Gemini 2.5 Flash) via declarative "modes", while targeted reads and reasoning stay on the frontier model. Boilerplate generation (tests, config stubs) follows the same path: the worker writes the output straight to disk so it never enters the frontier model's context. The reported result was a 90% token reduction on bulk reads. The pattern has three layers: hooks enforce the routing, scripts wrap the delegation calls, and skill files teach the agent when to use each path. The routing degrades gracefully: even if the agent ignores the skill description, the hook still blocks the expensive read (Spotify Engineering, Portal by Spotify cut my Claude Code token usage by 90% [114]).

            Evaluate the router type and current model list, rather than rejecting IPR categorically. The default-router support table still emphasizes Claude 3 / 3.5, Llama 3.x, and Nova Lite / Pro, while configured prompt routers can select additional supported models; the current AWS CLI example uses Claude Sonnet 4.5. Verify the models and Regions available when you design the route (Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing [28]; IPR product page [31], checked 10 September 2026).

            A gateway changes the cost-safety posture, and a cost runbook must say so plainly. AgentCore Gateway does not enforce a default maximum on response stream duration or size. So without an explicit token-limit policy configured per inference target, a single caller can exhaust the shared provider's tokens-per-minute quota and generate unbounded, maximum-cost responses. Those are the classic "noisy neighbour" and "cost amplification on shared credentials" failure modes (AgentCore inference connector targets, response stream limits [33]). Configure a per-target token-limit policy before you send production traffic, and confirm the current inference-target quotas (tokens- and requests-per-minute, maximum targets per gateway) on the limits page at design time (AgentCore service quotas [35]). Since 6 August 2026 that ceiling is a first-class gateway control rather than something you assemble. An AgentCore Gateway rate limit carrying a tokens metric caps tokens per minute on an inference target, and can be scoped per caller or per model (rate limit metrics [68]). The full pattern, including the two dimensions a token ceiling alone still leaves open, is covered in the Agent Harness layer (Guardrails and limits).

            Q2Do you audit pinned model IDs against the lifecycle pages?
            How to close this gap best practice

            The short answer. Keep an inventory of every pinned model ID and check it monthly against both the Bedrock and the Anthropic lifecycle pages; move off a model before Legacy turns into extended-access pricing.

            The plane that bills youWhere to checkWhat the states mean for cost
            Amazon Bedrock invocationThe Bedrock model-lifecycle page [16], or the modelLifecycle field of GetFoundationModel and ListFoundationModels.Active, then Legacy, then End-of-Life. Public extended access sits between Legacy and EOL, where active users keep calling at a higher, provider-set price until requests start failing at EOL.
            The Claude API and Claude for EnterpriseAnthropic's model-deprecations page [62], which lists retirement dates and recommended replacements.Active, then Legacy, then Deprecated, then Retired. The dates are independent of Bedrock, so the same model can be healthy on one plane and scheduled for retirement on the other.
            Read more for the self-serve reader

            Lifecycle audit. On Amazon Bedrock a model moves through Active, Legacy, and End-of-Life (EOL); read the current state from modelLifecycle in GetFoundationModel, and per-model dates from the Bedrock model-lifecycle guidance [16]. After at least three months in Legacy, a model enters public extended access at a higher, provider-set price. Anthropic publishes its own lifecycle (Active, Legacy, Deprecated, Retired) with independent schedules (Anthropic, Model deprecations [62]). The two schedules are independent, so check both if you invoke on both.

            What to do about it. Keep a small inventory of every pinned model ID in your fleet (Bedrock model ID and, where relevant, the Anthropic model name), and run a monthly check against both lifecycle pages. Move workloads off any model that has entered Legacy on either page before the extended-access price kicks in.

            What it saves: Blended bill under half the frontier-only baseline through tiered routing (worked example above). Lifecycle audit prevents Legacy pricing surprises.

            Route to the right price

            Challenge and why it costs

            Challenge. The same model on the same Region bills at different rates depending on the service tier, the inference mode, and the routing profile, yet most teams leave everything on Standard in a single Region because nobody made these explicit decisions.

            Why it costs. Development and test traffic that tolerates queuing pays the full interactive Standard price. Non-interactive, single-turn work that could run as a batch job consumes the interactive quota. A single-Region setup means throttling for callers in busy Regions with no automatic overflow, so latency-critical traffic on a model that offers Priority ends up on that tier at a 75% premium (Amazon Bedrock pricing [1]; CRIS pricing [22]).

            Assessment Answer each question for your workload, then open the guidance where you have a gap.
            Q1Do you choose Standard or batch deliberately for each workload?
            How to close this gap best practice

            The short answer. Default to Standard for anything a user waits on, and to batch, at half the price, for self-contained single-turn work the model supports. Check the model card before planning on Flex, Priority or Reserved.

            Your workModePrice vs Standard
            Anything a user is waiting onStandardbaseline
            Self-contained, single-turn, no-tool generation (bulk generation, offline eval scoring, nightly summarisation)Batch, where the model is in the support table50% cheaper, separate quota
            Tool-driven, structured-output or multi-turn workStandard; extract any independent generation step to batchbaseline
            Read more for the self-serve reader

            Best practice. Make the inference mode an explicit per-workload decision (Amazon Bedrock pricing [1]; AGENTCOST02-BP01 [11]).

            Batch inference is 50% cheaper than on-demand and runs on its own quota, so batched tokens stop drawing on the interactive TPM quota developers share during the day (Batch inference [37]). Its limits: it is asynchronous (submit a file of requests, read results from S3 hours later), it does not support tool calling or structured output, and it is per model. As of October 2026 the support table lists Claude 4.x and Opus 5 through cross-region inference profiles, but not Sonnet 5.x, GPT-5.x, or anything a user is waiting on (Supported Regions and models for batch inference [130]). Extract only the self-contained, single-turn, no-tool steps from mixed pipelines; keep the rest interactive.

            Other service tiers: check the model card for supported service tiers. Amazon Bedrock defines four tiers, but which ones a model supports is set per model and listed only in the Service Tiers section of its model card (Models at a glance [127]). For example, Claude Sonnet 5 supports the Standard tier only as of when this runbook was written (Claude Sonnet 5 model card, Service Tiers [128]); the OpenAI GPT-5.x cards say the same (GPT-5.6 Sol [129]), only the Claude 4.x generation lists Reserved, and Amazon Nova supports Flex and Priority. This changes at model launches, so check the card for each model you call before planning on a tier discount, and confirm what was actually served with the ResolvedServiceTier CloudWatch dimension (Bedrock service tiers [65]).

            Where a model does support them, the tier is one request parameter, service_tier, set to default, flex, priority or reserved [65]:

            TierWhat it is forPrice vs StandardQuota
            Standard (default)Everyday interactive traffic; where requests land when service_tier is omittedbaselineShared on-demand quota
            FlexQueue-tolerant work such as model evaluation, summarisation and agentic workflows that can wait50% cheaperShared on-demand quota; Flex changes the price, not the quota draw
            PriorityLatency-critical, customer-facing paths; served ahead of Standard and Flex75% dearerShared on-demand quota
            ReservedCommitted tokens-per-minute capacity for 1 or 3 months, set at account level with your AWS account team, overflowing to Standard when exceededfixed price per 1K TPMSeparate reservation, not on-demand
            Q2Do you call cross-region inference profiles rather than single-Region model IDs?
            How to close this gap best practice

            The short answer. Call a cross-region inference profile: Geographic where data residency requires it, Global (about 10% below the source-Region price) where it does not. You pay the source Region’s token price with no routing charge.

            ProfileWhere requests can runWhat you must configure, and the price
            GeographicWithin a single geography, which most compliance regimes require.Nothing beyond enabling the profile; standard source-Region price.
            GlobalAny commercial Region, including opt-in Regions where prompts and outputs can be stored for abuse detection (inference profiles [26]).An SCP that permits an unspecified aws:RequestedRegion. Approximately 10% below source Region.
            Read more for the self-serve reader

            Best practice. Cross-region inference sends each request to a Region that has capacity. You pay your source Region's per-token price, with no routing, data-transfer, or network charge (CRIS pricing [22]). A Geographic profile keeps routing within one geography at the standard price; a Global profile is documented at approximately 10% below source-Region price.

            In both cases data at rest stays in the source Region, and only transient compute crosses (CRIS security [27]). A throttled 429 is refused before inference runs, so it is not billed (429 errors [23]; on-demand billing [24]). Chronic throttling's real cost is user-facing latency and forced escalation to the Priority tier.

            What it saves: 50% on batch-eligible work, plus up to approximately 10% on a Global cross-region profile; Flex adds the same 50% on queue-tolerant traffic only where the model card lists it.

            Cache what repeats

            Challenge and why it costs

            Challenge. Every agentic call re-sends the same system prompt, tool definitions, and accumulated context. Without prompt caching, that repeated prefix is billed at the full input price on every turn of every session.

            Why it costs. Cache reads bill at roughly 0.1x the base input price, about a 90% discount on the cached portion (Amazon Bedrock pricing [1]), so an uncached workload pays up to ten times more than it needs to for its stable prefix; the Well-Architected Generative AI Lens recommends caching as a primary cost-optimisation practice (GENCOST03-BP03 [3]). Caching also fails silently: a reordered payload, a stripped checkpoint marker, or a timestamp added to the system prompt reverts every request to full price with no error, and the regression is only visible in the bill.

            Assessment Answer each question for your workload, then open the guidance where you have a gap.
            Q1Is prompt caching on, with the stable content placed first?
            How to close this gap best practice

            The short answer. Turn caching on and order the request so the stable content comes first: system prompt, then tool schemas, then reference documents, then the variable user turn. A read bills at about 0.1× the input price and a 5-minute write at 1.25×, so one re-read already pays for the write.

            Read more for the self-serve reader

            How to enable it. Place cache checkpoint markers in your request to tell Bedrock where the stable prefix ends. You get up to 4 checkpoints per request. Order them by how often each block changes: system prompt first (rarely changes), then tool schemas, then reference documents, then the variable user turn last. Only the content before the first variable section is cached (Bedrock prompt-caching documentation [5]; Anthropic prompt-caching documentation [6]).

            Key constraint: the write premium. The first write costs 1.25x (5-minute TTL) or 2x (1-hour TTL) of the base input price. Reads cost 0.1x. One re-read of a 5-minute write already saves more than three times the write premium. Anything that rewrites the prefix mid-session, including context pruning and compaction in the harness, pays that premium again; see Memory Q2 for when to prune.

            For a more recent Claude-specific study on maximising cache hit rates, removing prompt anti-patterns, and calibrating effort, see Anthropic, Reducing cost and improving performance with Claude Platform [115].

            Q2Have you verified caching works, and do you track the hit rate?
            How to close this gap best practice

            The short answer. Check that cacheReadInputTokens is non-zero from the second call of a session, then chart cache hit rate = cache reads / (cache reads + cache writes + uncached input) weekly per inference profile and alert when it drops.

            Common ways the cache silently breaks.

            • A dynamic value creeps into the stable prefix. The most frequent cause: a developer adds The current time is {timestamp} or a request ID into the system prompt for logging or debugging. Every request now has a unique prefix, so nothing matches the cache. Hit rate collapses to near-zero the day the change ships, but the invoice does not spike until month-end.
            • Tool schemas or reference documents change too often. Auto-refreshed tool catalogues, retrieved documents inserted before the stable block, or reordered system prompts all invalidate the cached prefix.
            Read more for the self-serve reader

            Why verification matters. Caching fails silently. If the prefix is too short, the payload is reordered, or a proxy between your agent and Bedrock strips the checkpoint markers, every request quietly reverts to full-price input with no error. Budget projections that assume the cache discount without checking are guesses.

            What to check first. Bedrock API responses include cacheReadInputTokens and cacheWriteInputTokens; per-profile CloudWatch metrics use CacheReadInputTokenCount and CacheWriteInputTokenCount. If cacheReadInputTokens is zero on the second and subsequent calls in a session, caching is not landing. Check at each layer: if an OpenAI-compatible shim or AgentCore Gateway sits between your agent and Bedrock, verify the metric at the Bedrock end, not just the proxy response (Bedrock prompt-caching documentation [5]).

            Track cache hit rate over time, not just at launch. Compute cache hit rate = cacheReadInputTokens / (cacheReadInputTokens + cacheWriteInputTokens + non-cached input tokens) per application inference profile, and chart it as a weekly time series alongside your spend. A hit rate that drifts down over weeks is a silent cost regression: input tokens quietly move from the 0.1x cache-read price back to the 1.0x base price, with no error and no alert.

            Alert when the weekly hit rate falls more than, say, 10 percentage points week over week, or below an absolute floor you set per workload. Otherwise these regressions are only visible in the bill.

            Q3Does your cache TTL match how often your sessions call?
            How to close this gap best practice

            The short answer. Use the 1-hour TTL (2× write) when users can pause for more than five minutes between calls, and the 5-minute default (1.25× write) for automated sessions that finish in seconds. A hit refreshes the TTL at no charge.

            Worked cost example

            Cache break-even for the supported Claude rates

            A 5-minute write bills at 1.25× base and a read at 0.1×. One read saves 0.9×, more than the 0.25× write premium, so the first re-read clears break-even. A 1-hour write at 2× base clears break-even after the second read. Check live model pricing before attaching a dollar figure (Bedrock pricing [1]).

            Read more for the self-serve reader

            Two TTL options. Bedrock offers a 5-minute TTL (default, 1.25x write cost) and a 1-hour TTL (2x write cost). The TTL refreshes on every cache hit at no additional charge, so a session that makes calls more frequently than the TTL window keeps the cache alive indefinitely (Bedrock prompt-caching documentation [5]).

            Which to choose. Interactive sessions where a user may pause for more than 5 minutes between actions should use the 1-hour TTL; otherwise the cache expires mid-session and the next call pays the full write premium again. Short-lived automated sessions (subagents, batch pipelines) that complete in seconds can stay on the cheaper 5-minute default.

            Cost trade-off. The 1-hour TTL costs 2x on the initial write vs 1.25x for 5-minute. But if the 5-minute cache expires and has to be rewritten, the second write wipes out the saving. Choose the TTL that avoids cache misses in your typical session pattern.

            What it saves: About 90% off repeated-prefix input (cache reads at 0.1x base), the single largest per-call saving for agentic workloads that re-send system prompts and tool definitions on every turn.

            Self-host or distill when volume justifies it

            Challenge and why it costs

            Challenge. Routing sends each request to the cheapest existing model that clears the quality bar, but for a high-volume, stable, well-defined task the cheapest existing small model may still miss the bar that a frontier model clears.

            Why it costs. That traffic then sits permanently on the expensive tier, paying frontier prices for a task whose shape never changes. Two paths convert that recurring premium into a fixed cost: self-host an open-weight model on infrastructure you own, or distill a smaller student model from the frontier teacher.

            Reality check first. Very few organisations get to this lever. Self-hosting an open-weight model (Llama, Mistral, DeepSeek) on your own infrastructure, or distilling a smaller student model from a frontier teacher, both ask for in-house ML or platform engineering capacity and access to enough compute (GPUs) to run training or inference. Self-hosting trades API simplicity for full control over weights, data residency, and per-token economics. Distillation goes further: it needs a large curated dataset to teach the student. If any of those inputs is missing, the earlier levers (route to the right model, route to the right price, cache what repeats) still have material savings left in them; come back here once volume, data, and staffing all line up.

            Real-world implementation. Goodnotes, the digital note-taking platform with over 24 million monthly active users, self-hosted an open-weight model on an Amazon EKS GPU cluster and cut inference costs by 97% compared to SaaS LLM APIs. The saving held while the team owned the GPU fleet and the user base fit within the cluster's capacity. When demand scaled to millions of concurrent users, operational overhead tipped the balance back toward the managed path, and the team migrated to Anthropic Claude on Amazon Bedrock. The lesson: self-hosting clears the break-even when you own the ops capacity to sustain it; when scaling outpaces your team, the managed path recaptures time that the token savings alone cannot buy back (Goodnotes case study, AWS [116]).

            Assessment Answer each question for your workload, then open the guidance where you have a gap.
            Q1Does your volume clear the break-even for distillation or self-hosting?
            How to close this gap best practice

            The short answer. Work out the break-even before the technique: months to break even = one-off training cost / monthly saving. Above about $500 a month and 10,000 invocations a month, customisation typically pays back within 6 to 12 months.

            Start with the break-even, not the technique: per the Agentic AI Lens, customization typically reaches break-even within 6 to 12 months above $500/month and 10,000 invocations/month (AGENTCOST02-BP04 [13]). The worked example: "for a $5,000 training run that saves $400 per month, break-even lands at month 13." Month 13 is acceptable for a workload with a multi-year lifespan and unacceptable for an experimental project.

            Q2Have you chosen the managed, managed-compute or self-managed path deliberately?
            How to close this gap best practice

            The short answer. Pick the path by how much control you need: managed Bedrock Model Distillation for the least engineering, SageMaker Training Jobs when you choose the student and its licence, and a self-managed HyperPod cluster only when you need a persistent cluster under your own control.

            PathChoose it whenHow it works
            Managed: Amazon Bedrock Model DistillationA supported student fits your task and you want the least engineering.Bedrock generates responses from a teacher model and uses them to fine-tune a cheaper student; you only provide prompts.
            Managed compute: SageMaker Training JobsYou need to pick an open-weight student and its licence, but do not want to run a persistent training cluster.Generate training data from your teacher, submit a Training Job with your chosen framework and training script; SageMaker provisions the GPUs, runs training, and tears the cluster down. Host on SageMaker or import to Bedrock via Custom Model Import.
            Self-managed: SageMaker HyperPod clusters + Custom Model ImportYou need a persistent cluster, custom topology, or long-running training under your control.Run your own HyperPod cluster, orchestrate training end-to-end, host on SageMaker or import to Bedrock. Confirm the student architecture is on the Custom Model Import supported list.
            Read more for the self-serve reader

            Three paths trade off engineering effort against control:

            • Managed distillation service: Amazon Bedrock Model Distillation. Least engineering. Bedrock generates responses from a teacher model and uses them to fine-tune a cheaper student; you only provide prompts. Confirm your student choice is on the supported list.
            • Managed compute: SageMaker Training Jobs. SageMaker provisions and tears down the training cluster; you keep control of the student family, the training code, and the licence, without operating a persistent GPU fleet. Fits teams that want to distil an open-weight student (Llama, Mistral, DeepSeek) but do not want to run their own cluster (SageMaker Training Jobs [117]).
            • Self-managed cluster: SageMaker HyperPod clusters + Custom Model Import. Most control, most operational overhead. Choose this when you need a persistent cluster, custom topology, or long-running training that must sit entirely under your control (Effective cost optimization strategies for Amazon Bedrock [12]; Bedrock Custom Model Import [51]).
            Q3Do you curate the training data, A/B test the student and plan a refresh?
            How to close this gap best practice

            The short answer. Train only on high-confidence successful production completions, A/B test the student against the teacher before promoting it, and budget a refresh cadence so the student does not drift.

            Read more for the self-serve reader

            Curate training prompts from production logs filtered for high-confidence successful completions, A/B test the distilled model against the foundation model before promoting it, and budget a refresh cadence. Confirm supported teacher/student pairs on the live Bedrock Model Distillation documentation [14].

            What it saves: Break-even in 6 to 12 months above the thresholds. It converts a recurring per-invocation premium into a one-time training cost (distillation) or a fixed fleet cost you control (self-hosting); the cited thresholds are >$500/month and >10,000 invocations/month.

              No gaps recorded yet. Answer the questions above and any Not covered or Partially items will appear here.

              Agent Harness

              How the harness multiplies cost. The model determines the price of one invocation. The harness determines how many invocations a task makes and how much context each invocation carries. Use the cost model below to identify which multiplier dominates before choosing a lever.

              Challenge and why it costs

              Challenge. An agent loop does not bill like a chat. A task that takes N tool-call rounds re-sends the accumulating context on every round, so the same tokens are billed again and again as the loop runs.

              Why it costs. Model the cost of one task as cost per task ≈ rounds × average context size × input price (plus output). Every extra round both adds a multiplication and grows the average context it multiplies, because each round appends its tool results to the context the next round re-sends; total input tokens therefore grow roughly with the square of the round count, not linearly. The mechanism is architectural: transformer attention creates "n² pairwise relationships for n tokens" (Anthropic engineering, Effective context engineering for AI agents [38], Sep 2025), and the same growth that inflates the bill also degrades recall as context lengthens, which Anthropic calls context rot. Long, expensive contexts are worse contexts.

              Include in this assessment: Agent Harness

              Untick a lever that does not apply to your workload. Its questions are hidden and left out of every count, summary and export; the choice is saved in this browser. Clicking a box in the figure above does the same.

              System prompt

              Challenge and why it costs

              Challenge. The system prompt is re-sent on every model call in the loop, so it is the largest fixed cost of an invocation. It grows by accretion: every incident adds a sentence and nothing removes one.

              Why it costs. Every token in a system prompt is paid for on every invocation, so prompt bloat compounds linearly with traffic (AGENTCOST02-BP02 [83]). A padded prompt is also a larger cache prefix to write, and a volatile value placed inside it, such as a timestamp or a user name, breaks the cache on every call, so the discount you planned on is never collected (Bedrock prompt caching [5]).

              Assessment Answer each question for your workload, then open the guidance where you have a gap.
              Q1Is your system prompt as lean as it can be?
              How to close this gap best practice

              The short answer. The fixed cost of a task is system prompt tokens × model calls per task × input price, paid before the user says a word. Measure the prompt in tokens, strip persona padding and redundant explanation, and keep only the instructions the behaviour needs.

              Worked example

              The same 15-call task under four system prompts

              One task takes 15 model calls. Cache reads bill at 0.1× the input price and a 5-minute cache write at 1.25×; the dollar column uses an illustrative $3 per million input tokens. “Billed token-equivalents” weights each token by the rate it was billed at, so the rows compare directly.

              ConfigurationPrompt tokensBilled token-equivalents per taskCost per taskAgainst the baseline
              Padded prompt, no caching (baseline)2,00030,000$0.090baseline
              Padded prompt, caching on, but a timestamp on the first line (the common mistake: every call is a cache write, none is a read)2,00037,500$0.11325% worse
              Padded prompt, caching on, stable prefix2,0005,300$0.01682% saved
              Trimmed to the minimum, caching on, stable prefix (best practice)8002,120$0.00693% saved

              The arithmetic: 2,000 × 15 = 30,000 uncached; 2,000 × 1.25 × 15 = 37,500 when every call rewrites the cache; 2,000 × 1.25 + 14 × 2,000 × 0.1 = 5,300 when the prefix holds; 800 × 1.25 + 14 × 800 × 0.1 = 2,120 once the prompt is trimmed as well. The second row is the point: caching that is switched on but never hits costs more than no caching at all, and the invoice is the first place it shows (Bedrock prompt caching [5]; AGENTCOST02-BP02 [83]).

              Read more for the self-serve reader

              Minimum, not short. The goal is the smallest set of instructions that still produces the behaviour you need, not the fewest words. Start with a minimal prompt on the most capable model, measure where it fails, and add instructions and examples only for the failure modes you observed. Strip persona descriptions, restated context and explanations the model does not need (Effective context engineering for AI agents [38]; AGENTCOST02-BP02 [83]).

              Right altitude. Avoid both extremes: brittle if-then logic written out in prose, and vague guidance that assumes shared context. Give the model strong heuristics and tell it why, and organise the prompt into labelled sections (background, instructions, tool guidance, output format) so each instruction is found once (Effective context engineering for AI agents [38]; Anthropic, Claude 4 prompting best practices [134]).

              Examples are paid for on every call. Test zero-shot first. Where examples are needed, two or three canonical ones usually suffice; retrieve them per task from a library rather than embedding every edge case for every task (AGENTCOST02-BP02 [83]; Effective context engineering for AI agents [38]).

              Constrain the output in the prompt. State the response structure and a maximum length, and set the model’s token limit parameter as a hard cap, because output tokens compound across the rounds of a loop (AGENTCOST02-BP02 [83]).

              A starting allocation, not a target. The Agentic AI Lens suggests budgeting the context window as roughly 20 to 30% system prompt, 30 to 40% user context, 10 to 20% examples and 20 to 30% scratchpad, then adjusting to the agent’s observed reasoning pattern (AGENTCOST02-BP02 [83]).

              Q2Is your system prompt versioned and cache-stable?
              How to close this gap best practice

              The short answer. Treat the prompt as a versioned artefact: record token count, task success and cost per task for every version, and keep the prefix byte-stable, with volatile values (date, user, session id) placed after it, so the cache survives every call.

              Read more for the self-serve reader

              Keep the prefix stable for the cache. Bedrock and Anthropic cache the request in order: tools, then system prompt, then messages. Any value that changes per request and sits in or before the system prompt (the current time, a user name, a request id added for logging) invalidates everything after it. Put volatile content in the first user message instead, and treat any edit to the system prompt as a cache-rewrite event that will show as a one-day dip in hit rate (Bedrock prompt caching [5]; Anthropic prompt caching [6]).

              Version and measure. Store the prompt as a versioned artefact rather than a string in code, and for each version record its token count, task success rate and cost per task, so a change that quietly doubles tokens per task is caught in review rather than in the bill. Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management provides versions and variants (Bedrock Prompt Management [131]), its prompt optimizer produces a measured rewrite you can compare against the current version (Optimize a prompt [132]), and the Generative AI Lens treats versioned prompt templates with a baseline evaluation as the operating standard (GENOPS03-BP01 [133]; AGENTCOST02-BP02 [83]).

              Review on a cadence. A monthly review that compares cost per task across prompt versions, alongside the cache hit rate in Cache what repeats, keeps compression an ongoing practice instead of a one-off clean-up (AGENTCOST02-BP02 [83]).

              What it saves: Up to about 90% of the prompt’s share of input when a trimmed prompt is also cache-stable (worked example above). The trim alone saves in proportion to the tokens removed, on every call of every task.

              Context

              Challenge and why it costs

              Challenge. The harness assembles instructions, retrieved material, conversation history, memory and tool results into every model request. Without an explicit lifecycle, the working set grows by default.

              Why it costs. Every token that remains in the working set is billed again on later rounds. Append-only history, full tool results and oversized checkpoints make cost grow with session length rather than task complexity.

              Assessment Answer each question for your workload, then open the guidance where you have a gap.
              Q1Do you measure and budget what each request’s context contains?
              How to close this gap best practice

              The short answer. Measure before you cut: input tokens per call = instructions + capability definitions + working context + runtime output + retained state. Record each source’s tokens and how many rounds it survives; whatever is both large and carried across rounds is billed again on every round.

              Context sourceWhat to measure
              Stable instructionsSystem prompts, organisation guidance and repository instructions.
              Capability definitionsTool, skill and MCP descriptions and schemas.
              Working contextRetrieved material, recent conversation and active task state.
              Runtime outputTool results, files, logs and browser output.
              Retained stateSummaries, memory retrieved for the task and checkpoint data.
              Read more for the self-serve reader

              Measure the context before trying to reduce it. Break each request into the sources that contribute input tokens.

              Record the token contribution of each source and how long it remains in the working context. Prioritise content that is both large and carried across many rounds, because it is billed repeatedly.

              Q2Are tool and runtime outputs bounded before they enter the context?
              How to close this gap best practice

              The short answer. Give every tool an output contract: return the smallest result that supports the next decision, with a pointer to the rest, so a file read, a log search or a page snapshot cannot flood the context.

              Runtime operationPreferAvoid
              File readingRequested line range, matching sections or a diffAn entire large file
              Log searchMatching errors, bounded context and a maximum match countAn unlimited log stream
              Repository searchRanked snippets with paginationEvery matching file and its full contents
              Browser inspectionRelevant fields or an accessibility snapshotComplete page source when only one value is needed
              Sandbox executionStatus, key output, bounded error tail and artifact pathsUnbounded standard output
              Read more for the self-serve reader
              Bound what each capability returns

              Give every runtime operation an explicit output contract. Return the smallest result that supports the next decision, together with a pointer or continuation token when more detail remains available.

              Measure direct runtime cost separately from context cost. Track API calls or execution duration for the first, then p50 and p95 result tokens, truncation frequency and follow-up requests for the second. If consumers repeatedly request omitted detail, increase the bound carefully rather than removing it.

              Anthropic recommends token-efficient tools and just-in-time retrieval instead of loading complete data objects into context (Effective context engineering for AI agents [38]). AWS Prescriptive Guidance identifies excessive tool invocation as a direct runtime cost driver (APG, Agentic AI cost optimisation [7]).

              What it saves: Keeps per-round input bounded, so context cost tracks the task rather than the age of the session.

              Memory shared

              Challenge and why it costs

              Challenge. Conversation history, tool results and checkpoints accumulate by default. Without a memory policy, the working set grows with every turn.

              Why it costs. Every retained token is billed again on each later round, so append-only history makes cost track the length of the session rather than the complexity of the task (AGENTCOST03 [40]). Compaction done carelessly rewrites the cached prefix and pays the write premium again (Bedrock prompt caching [5]).

              Assessment Answer each question for your workload, then open the guidance where you have a gap.
              Q1Have you chosen how history is kept, instead of append-only?
              How to close this gap best practice

              The short answer. Decide how the agent remembers before the history grows: a fixed window, rolling summaries, or retrieval from external memory. Append-only history makes cost grow with the age of the session rather than the size of the task.

              ArchitectureHow it worksTrade-off
              Fixed-window truncationKeeps the most recent turns and removes older ones.Cheapest and simplest, but may discard an earlier decision.
              Rolling summarisationReplaces older history with a shorter summary.Bounds context growth, but adds summarisation cost and may omit detail.
              Semantic memory with retrievalStores structured information outside the active context and retrieves it when relevant.Keeps the working context small, but adds storage, retrieval and relevance risk.
              Read more for the self-serve reader

              Choose how the agent will retain information before the history becomes large. The appropriate approach depends on how far back the task must remember and how costly an omitted detail would be. The Agentic AI Lens sets the goal as sessions that “compress and prune history continually, keeping token cost sub-linear as conversation length grows” (AGENTCOST03 [40]).

              For long-running work, Anthropic describes compaction as an early context-engineering control because it can retain architectural decisions and unresolved issues while removing redundant tool output (Effective context engineering for AI agents [38]).

              On supported Anthropic models, server-side compaction and context editing can clear older tool-use and thinking blocks after configurable thresholds (Anthropic, Context editing [64]). The user-managed counterpart is Track 1's Manage the session and its context actively.

              Memory management and prompt caching solve different problems. Memory management reduces the amount of changing history sent with each call. Prompt caching reduces the price of stable content sent unchanged. Use both, but avoid rewriting the stable prefix during compaction because that can cause a cache miss.

              Q2Do you prune at natural boundaries, without breaking the cache every turn?
              How to close this gap best practice

              The short answer. Prune at natural boundaries (task completion, an idle gap longer than the cache TTL, a size threshold), not every turn, because each prune rewrites the cached prefix and pays the write premium again. Keep the conclusion, drop the raw material.

              ContentRetain
              Large tool outputThe relevant result, error, excerpt or summary.
              Changed code or configurationA diff or changed lines rather than complete before-and-after files.
              Prior conversationA recent window plus the summary or retrieved memory selected by the memory policy.
              Checkpoint stateDecisions, unresolved work and restart data rather than the complete transcript.
              Read more for the self-serve reader
              Prune consumed context

              Remove or reduce content once the agent has extracted what it needs. Preserve the useful conclusion, not the complete raw material that produced it.

              Set the history bound from observed task behaviour. If tasks rarely refer to older turns, carrying them forward adds cost without value. Do not compact too frequently, because summarisation is itself a model call. Compare the tokens removed with the tokens spent producing the summary.

              Pruning rewrites the cached prefix. Prompt caching only pays when the prefix is byte-identical between requests; editing an earlier turn or clearing a tool result changes the prefix from that point on, so the next call misses the cache and re-writes it at the cache-write premium (Bedrock prompt caching [5]). Prune at natural boundaries rather than every turn: task completion, before an idle gap longer than the cache TTL, or when context crosses a size threshold. Prefer appending a summary to editing history where the harness allows it, and weigh the tokens removed against the re-cache cost, not only against the summary cost. See Cache what repeats for the write premium and TTLs.

              This is the builder-controlled version of context hygiene. Implementing it in the harness applies the policy consistently instead of relying on every user to manage context manually. See Track 1's Manage the session and its context actively for the user-managed counterpart.

              What it saves: Sub-linear history cost: the context sent per call stops growing with the age of the session, and compaction at boundaries keeps the cache discount intact.

              Tool design shared

              Challenge and why it costs

              Challenge. Every tool, skill, MCP operation and bundled execution facility expands what the agent can invoke. Definitions add standing context, while invocations add runtime cost and results that may enter later model calls.

              Why it costs. A broad catalogue raises the fixed input floor, and unbounded filesystem, sandbox or browser output can dominate the working context long after the tool call completed.

              Assessment Answer each question for your workload, then open the guidance where you have a gap.
              Q1Do you keep a costed inventory of tools, skills and MCP servers?
              How to close this gap best practice

              The short answer. Keep a versioned inventory of every tool, skill and MCP operation with an owner, a use case, its definition tokens and its measured runtime cost. definition tokens × calls per task is a fixed tax on every task.

              Review itemPractical action
              Purpose and ownerGive every capability one clear use case and an accountable owner. Remove entries without a current use case.
              Functional overlapCombine tools such as find_order and search_orders when their inputs and results overlap, or define a clear boundary between them.
              Definition weightCount tokens in the serialized name, description and parameter schema. Remove tutorials, repeated examples and implementation detail that do not help tool selection.
              Runtime costRecord direct API or compute cost, calls per successful workflow and typical result size.
              EvidenceAfter catalogue changes, compare task success, input tokens, tool-selection errors, retries and cost per successful workflow on representative tasks.
              Read more for the self-serve reader
              Audit the capability catalogue

              Maintain a versioned inventory of every capability available to the agent. Measure the actual definitions sent to the model because frameworks package tool metadata differently.

              Do not optimise for the fewest tools alone. Keep the smallest catalogue that completes representative tasks reliably.

              AWS recommends keeping tool descriptions at the minimum size required for accurate decisions and warns that unreviewed tool catalogues create a growing fixed input-token cost (AGENTCOST02 [4]). Anthropic similarly recommends clear, self-contained tools with minimal functional overlap (Effective context engineering for AI agents [38]).

              Q2Does each call see only the tools it needs?
              How to close this gap best practice

              The short answer. Separate the full registry from what one request carries: load a small core set plus the capabilities the current intent needs, and keep the rest out of the context.

              Current intentExposeWithhold
              Answer a documentation questionDocumentation search and read operationsDeployment, administration and write operations
              Investigate a failed buildSource search, log reading and test executionProduction deployment and unrelated business systems
              Process a returnOrder lookup, policy lookup and return creationInfrastructure, browser automation and unrelated customer operations
              Read more for the self-serve reader
              Load capabilities for the current task

              Separate the complete capability registry from the definitions placed in a model request. The registry records everything the application can use; the context builder selects what the current invocation needs.

              For a large or changing catalogue, use semantic tool selection or a lightweight classifier. Retain a small core set for routing and recovery, then load specialised capabilities when needed. If intent is uncertain, allow progressive discovery or include a borderline capability rather than forcing failure and retry.

              Measure definition tokens per invocation, task success, tool-selection errors, missing-capability retries and net cost per successful workflow. AWS recommends dynamically presenting task-relevant tools and describes AgentCore Gateway Semantic Tool Selection as one implementation (AGENTCOST02-BP02 [83]).

              What it saves: Lowers the fixed capability tax and prevents runtime output from becoming recurring context.

              Orchestration

              Challenge and why it costs

              Challenge. The orchestrator decides when to invoke a model, retry, delegate, synthesise and stop. Multi-agent designs multiply those decisions across workers and supervisors.

              Why it costs. Every unnecessary branch, retry, hierarchy level and handoff adds model calls or moves context before the workflow produces an outcome.

              Assessment Answer each question for your workload, then open the guidance where you have a gap.
              Q1Do loops have termination and retry limits, with rules where rules suffice?
              How to close this gap best practice

              The short answer. Put the stopping, retry and routing rules in code: an iteration cap, a session token budget, a completion exit, retries only for transient failures, and a deterministic branch wherever the inputs decide it.

              ControlWhat to implementPractical example
              TerminationSet an iteration cap, a session token budget and a completion or confidence exit.Stop after eight tool rounds, when the token budget is spent, or as soon as all acceptance criteria pass.
              RetriesRetry only failures classified as transient, with a maximum attempt count and a terminal path for repeated failure.Retry a timeout twice, but do not repeat a request rejected for an invalid parameter.
              RoutingUse code for deterministic branches, a lightweight classifier for narrow ambiguity and a supervisor model only for decisions needing language understanding.Route by status, file type or numeric threshold without invoking a model.
              Read more for the self-serve reader
              Bound control flow in harness code

              Put stopping, retry and routing rules in the harness rather than relying on the model to regulate itself. Each rule should be explicit, observable and independently testable.

              Route deterministically before invoking a supervisor

              If the inputs fully decide the branch, encode the decision as a rule. Reserve model supervision for genuinely ambiguous intent or planning decisions. AWS identifies missing iteration limits, unnecessary model-based routing and overly deep orchestration as common causes of unpredictable token consumption (AGENTCOST01 [39]).

              Q2Is multi-agent used only where it beats a single agent?
              How to close this gap best practice

              The short answer. Establish a single-agent baseline first. multi-agent cost ≈ N × (worker context + worker execution) + coordination + synthesis, so add workers only for independently divisible work, and have them hand back distilled results, not transcripts.

              Design testWhat to doPractical example
              Independent divisibilitySplit work only when workers do not depend on unfinished results or compete to modify the same state.Search three independent evidence sources in parallel; keep a sequential refactor of one file with one agent.
              Context isolationGive each worker only its task, ready inputs, constraints and acceptance criteria.Let a log-analysis worker inspect the full log, then return the failure signature and supporting lines rather than its complete exploration.
              Structured handoffDefine a compact payload containing the task, inputs, output schema, acceptance criteria and unresolved issues.Pass a result object or artifact reference instead of replaying the parent conversation.
              Shallow topologyUse the fewest supervision and synthesis layers the workflow needs.Allow an independent worker to complete its bounded subtask without reporting to a supervisor after every tool call.
              Baseline comparisonCompare task success, elapsed time, total tokens, retries and total cost with the single-agent run.Keep the multi-agent design only when its measured benefit is worth its added cost.
              Read more for the self-serve reader
              Make multi-agent execution earn its overhead

              Establish a single-agent baseline before adding workers. Parallelise only work that can proceed independently and whose latency or outcome benefit justifies the additional context, coordination and synthesis.

              Minimise multi-agent handoff payloads

              A worker can explore a large context and return only a distilled result to the parent. Anthropic describes subagents that use tens of thousands of tokens internally but return summaries of about 1,000 to 2,000 tokens, preventing the full exploration from entering the main session history (Effective context engineering for AI agents [38]).

              Use the simplified estimate multi-agent cost ≈ N × (worker context + worker execution) + coordination + synthesis. More workers are not a free speed-up: each worker receives context, and the workflow still pays to dispatch, coordinate and combine their results.

              Q3Do you measure the full cost of a workflow, including retries and coordination?
              How to close this gap best practice

              The short answer. Instrument the whole workflow, not just the worker calls: execution, retries, idempotency, checkpointing, coordination and synthesis, per workflow version and per outcome. Trend the orchestration-to-execution token ratio.

              Cost componentWhat to measureWhat it reveals
              ExecutionWorker model tokens, tool calls and direct runtime charges.The cost of useful task work.
              RetriesRepeated model and tool calls, grouped by failure type and attempt.Retry amplification and failures that should terminate rather than repeat.
              IdempotencyState writes, prior-completion checks and compensating operations.The standing cost of making selected steps safe to repeat.
              CheckpointingState serialisation, storage, retrieval and the size of each checkpoint.Whether durable recovery stores distilled state or duplicates full context.
              CoordinationDispatch, routing, supervisor and handoff tokens and calls.Overhead added before workers produce useful output.
              SynthesisTokens and calls used to combine, evaluate or reconcile worker results.The cost paid after parallel work completes.
              Read more for the self-serve reader
              Measure total orchestration cost

              Instrument the complete workflow rather than measuring worker model calls alone. Attribute each cost to a workflow version and successful or failed outcome so architecture changes can be compared on the same basis.

              Track total tokens and total cost per successful workflow. Also trend the orchestration-to-execution token ratio, using coordination and synthesis tokens as the numerator and useful worker-execution tokens as the denominator. There is no universal target: compare later releases with a known-good baseline, and investigate when the ratio rises while task complexity and success remain stable.

              AWS recommends measuring reasoning and orchestration costs against successful outcomes because retries, handoffs and hierarchy can multiply spend without improving decision quality (AGENTCOST01 [39]).

              What it saves: Bounds the orchestration multiplier, removing avoidable calls and keeping coordination proportional to useful work.

              Guardrails and limits

              Challenge and why it costs

              Challenge. A termination rule limits one workflow, but it does not constrain how many workflows run concurrently or how several callers consume shared capacity.

              Why it costs. Queue drains, tenant fan-out and shared credentials can multiply otherwise controlled per-workflow cost across the system.

              Assessment Answer each question for your workload, then open the guidance where you have a gap.
              Q1Are concurrency, queue depth and fan-out bounded in dispatcher code?
              How to close this gap best practice

              The short answer. A termination rule makes one workflow finite; dispatcher limits (queue depth, worker count, concurrency, fan-out width) decide how many finite workflows run at once. Enforce them in code, not in prompts.

              Burst sourceControl to implementPractical outcome
              Queue backlogSet a maximum queue depth and an explicit admission or deferral policy.A backlog cannot become an unlimited inventory of future model calls.
              Worker poolSet a maximum worker count and apply backpressure when the pool is full.A queue drain cannot start every waiting workflow at once.
              Concurrent tasksSet global and, where needed, per-tenant concurrency ceilings.One tenant cannot occupy the complete worker pool.
              Fan-outSet the maximum child-task count in dispatcher configuration.The width is reviewed as code rather than chosen dynamically by a prompt.
              Read more for the self-serve reader
              Cap aggregate consumption in dispatcher code

              The termination controls in Orchestration make one workflow finite. Dispatcher limits control how many finite workflows can consume resources at the same time. Enforce these ceilings in code rather than prompts.

              Size each limit using observed legitimate demand and the cost budget for the workload. Review it when traffic, model choice, context size or workflow design changes. A ceiling set too high provides little containment; one set too low creates avoidable throttling and retries.

              Q2Are request, token and connection limits enforced per caller at the gateway?
              How to close this gap best practice

              The short answer. At the gateway, limit requests, tokens and connections per caller, tenant or target, keyed to an identity the gateway already validates. Request count alone does not describe request cost.

              DimensionWhat it containsWhy it is needed
              RequestsCalls per second or minute.Contains high-frequency loops and retry storms.
              TokensInput plus output tokens over a time window.Contains expensive requests that remain within a request-count limit.
              ConnectionsConcurrent long-lived sessions.Contains slow sessions that hold capacity while sending few requests.
              Read more for the self-serve reader
              Isolate shared consumption at the gateway

              Dispatcher limits cover paths your application owns. A gateway or proxy adds a common enforcement point for agents and callers that share targets or provider credentials. Limit each relevant consumption dimension because request count alone does not describe request cost.

              Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway supports request, token and connection rate limits. Token limits apply to supported inference paths, while request and connection limits apply more broadly (Control agent behaviors and cost [71]; AgentCore inference connector targets [33]).

              Key limits to an identity or resource your gateway already validates. Examples include an OAuth subject, role or authorized party; an IAM principal or source identity; and a target, tool or model identifier. A wildcard dimension can give each distinct caller its own bucket without pre-registering every caller (Add rate limits to a gateway [67]; rate limit metrics [68]).

              Validate the limit
              • Test fail-open behaviour. AgentCore rate limits allow requests to proceed if the limiter is unavailable or a dimension cannot be resolved, so retain dispatcher limits and authorization controls.
              • Check service quotas. The effective ceiling cannot exceed the underlying service-managed limit.
              • Verify identity resolution. Test every authentication path and confirm the intended caller receives an isolated bucket.
              • Verify attribution. Confirm throttle telemetry identifies enough context to investigate the responsible caller; use harness invocation tracing where it does not.
              • Tune with evidence. Review throttling, retries and legitimate demand when changing models, traffic patterns or limit values.

              Optional defence in depth. Where a runaway workflow can repeat high-impact actions, AgentCore temporal policies can enforce a session-scoped action count or cumulative value outside the harness. This constrains blast radius; it does not replace token budgets or rate limits (Temporal policies [69]; Authoring temporal policies [70]).

              What it saves: Caps aggregate and per-caller consumption, preventing concurrent workflows or one shared caller from multiplying otherwise controlled cost.

              Observability

              Challenge and why it costs

              Challenge. Not every model or tool invocation traces back to work somebody requested. Loops can continue after completion, retries can repeat permanent failures, and scheduled jobs or health checks can invoke models without a user task.

              Why it costs. These calls look legitimate in aggregate usage, but produce no valid task outcome. Without task-level correlation and reconciliation, they can continue until a billing review exposes them.

              Assessment Answer each question for your workload, then open the guidance where you have a gap.
              Q1Can you trace every model and tool call to its caller and task?
              How to close this gap best practice

              The short answer. Stamp caller, task, workflow and harness version on every model and tool call when work enters the harness, and turn on Bedrock model invocation logging, which is off by default.

              FieldWhat it identifiesPractical use
              CallerThe user, service, scheduler or system component that initiated the work.Separates interactive work from background callers.
              TaskThe requested unit of work and its current outcome.Shows whether an invocation belongs to valid work.
              WorkflowThe workflow type, run and step that issued the invocation.Locates loops, retries and expensive branches.
              Harness versionThe deployed configuration or code version controlling the run.Connects a traffic change to a release.
              Read more for the self-serve reader
              Attach a correlation contract to every invocation

              Generate the identifiers when work enters the harness and propagate them through every model call, tool call, retry, worker and synthesis step. Do not reconstruct them later from timestamps or log text.

              Enable Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging in the invoking account because it is disabled by default. It can record supported Bedrock Runtime requests and the calling principal in identity.arn; add task, workflow and harness-version identifiers in your own harness telemetry (Bedrock model invocation logging [47]).

              Q2Do you reconcile invocations against requested work to find orphans?
              How to close this gap best practice

              The short answer. Join invocation records to the task ledger. Any call with no valid task, after a terminal outcome, or above the configured calls per task is a finding, not usage.

              Invocation patternLikely cause
              Calls without a valid task or correlation identifierAn orphaned caller or untracked integration.
              Calls continuing after a terminal task outcomeA runaway loop, stale worker or scheduler that was not cancelled.
              The same failed step repeatingA retry storm around a permanent failure.
              Regular calls without a corresponding user sessionA scheduled job or model-backed health check.
              Calls per task above the configured workflow limitA termination or retry control failure.
              Read more for the self-serve reader
              Reconcile invocations against the task ledger

              Join model and tool invocation records to the harness task ledger using the correlation identifiers from Q1. Every invocation should map to a requested task, a valid workflow step and the task state at the time of the call. Treat an unmatched or post-completion invocation as a finding rather than allocating it to aggregate usage.

              Review the highest-volume unmatched pattern first. The objective is not to reduce valid task traffic; it is to find invocations that should not have occurred.

              Q3Do you alert on calls with no task, after completion, or over budget?
              How to close this gap best practice

              The short answer. Publish the reconciliation as metrics and alert on contract violations (unmatched calls, post-completion calls, calls per task over the limit), routed to the owner of that workflow and harness version.

              SignalHow to use it
              Unmatched invocationsAlert when any production call lacks a valid task, workflow or caller identifier.
              Post-completion invocationsAlert when a workflow continues after success, failure or cancellation.
              Calls per taskCompare with the workflow's configured iteration and retry limits.
              Repeated failure signaturesDetect retries that repeat the same terminal error without changing inputs.
              Background-call volumeTrack scheduled and health-check traffic separately from user-requested work.
              Read more for the self-serve reader
              Turn reconciliation findings into continuous signals

              Publish metrics from the reconciliation in Q2 and alert on violations of your harness contracts rather than on a universal invocation threshold.

              Route each alert to the owner of the workflow and harness version identified in Q1. Use Orchestration to correct loop and retry controls, and use Know what you spend and what it buys for financial attribution and release economics.

              What it saves: Eliminates work no valid task required, exposing orphaned loops, retry storms and forgotten background callers before they become persistent traffic.
