                End User

                Include in this assessment: End User

                Untick a lever that does not apply to your workload. Its questions are hidden and left out of every count, summary and export; the choice is saved in this browser. Clicking a box in the figure above does the same.

                Precise specifications to avoid rework

                Challenge and why it costs

                Challenge. A vague request leaves the agent to infer the required output, constraints, edge cases and scope. The first result may be plausible but still solve the wrong problem.

                Why it costs. Each correction repeats exploration and generation, re-sends accumulated context and consumes fresh output tokens for the same logical task.

                Assessment Answer the question for your workload, then open the guidance where you have a gap.
                Q1Do users specify output, constraints and scope before the agent starts?
                How to close this gap best practice

                The short answer. Ask users to state five things before the agent starts: the required output, constraints, edge cases, one example, and what is out of scope. Every correction round re-sends the whole context, so a one-minute specification is cheaper than one retry.

                Specification elementWhat to statePractical example
                Required outputThe deliverable, format and level of detail.Produce a one-page decision summary with a comparison table.
                ConstraintsRules, technologies, budgets or compatibility requirements.Use the existing API and do not add a dependency.
                Edge casesInputs or failure conditions that must be handled.Include empty results, timeouts and partial failures.
                ExamplesA representative input and acceptable output when wording alone may be ambiguous.Show one correctly formatted record.
                Out of scopeWork the agent must not perform.Do not change the database schema or deployment configuration.
                Read more for the self-serve reader
                Write a short specification before execution

                Front-load the information the agent would otherwise have to discover through clarifying questions or failed attempts. The specification can be brief, but it should make success and failure observable.

                For larger tasks, use a planning pass to test assumptions and sequence the work before execution. Track 1 applies the same habit in Plan before executing complex work. AWS Prescriptive Guidance similarly treats avoiding wasted and redundant calls as a core agentic cost practice (APG, Agentic AI cost optimisation [7]).

                What it saves: Prevents avoidable correction rounds, reducing repeated exploration and generation caused by missing requirements.

                Guided prompting to reduce input ambiguity

                Challenge and why it costs

                Challenge. The Precise specifications lever above puts the burden of precision on the user: write a clear, complete prompt and you avoid rework. When you build and operate the application, you do not have to wait for the user to be precise. Left to type into a blank box, users are ambiguous by default, and every ambiguous free-text turn is one the agent may have to explore, guess at, and redo.

                Why it costs. An ambiguous request triggers the same explore, generate, and retry cycle that a vague specification does: the agent produces something approximate, the user corrects it, and the model re-runs the task, each round re-billing the input context and burning fresh output tokens. Multiplied across a fleet of users who each phrase the same intent a dozen different ways, that variance is a standing rework tax the application pays on every session.

                Assessment Answer each question for your workload, then open the guidance where you have a gap.
                Q1Does your interface offer clickable options instead of a blank text box?
                How to close this gap best practice

                The short answer. Offer suggested follow-ups, quick replies or slot filling, so the user selects a precise next request instead of typing an ambiguous one.

                PatternWhat the application does
                Suggested follow-upsProposes the likely next step at the end of a turn as a clickable, well-formed prompt, so the user selects a precise next request instead of typing an ambiguous one.
                Quick repliesOffers a constrained set of tappable responses, replacing an open-ended answer with one the agent can act on directly.
                Slot filling (structured elicitation)Elicits the specific parameters the task needs, one field at a time, rather than accepting a single open-ended sentence.
                Read more for the self-serve reader

                Because you own the UX and the invocation, you can make precision the path of least resistance rather than a discipline you hope the user keeps. Guided prompting is the builder-owned complement to Precise specifications: the application anticipates the user's likely next request and surfaces well-formed, clickable options instead of relying on free-text entry. All three established patterns are applications of choice architecture, because constraining the option set nudges the user toward inputs the agent can act on in a single pass.

                Q2Are those inputs low-variance, so clarifying round-trips are rare?
                How to close this gap best practice

                The short answer. Design each option so the agent can act on it in one pass. A predictable input removes the clarifying call and the redo.

                Read more for the self-serve reader

                Across suggested follow-ups, quick replies and slot filling, the goal is to replace ambiguous free text with a small set of predictable inputs. This reduces the need for clarifying questions and repeated model calls. The same front-loaded-precision principle is anchored in AWS Prescriptive Guidance for serverless agentic AI, which treats minimising wasted and redundant calls as a core cost lever (APG, Agentic AI cost optimisation [7]).

                What it saves: Cuts clarifying round-trips at the source, converting ambiguous, high-variance free-text turns into precise inputs and removing rework cycles before they start. It is the builder-owned complement to the user-owned Precise specifications lever, applied by the application rather than left to the user (qualitative; the magnitude tracks how much of your traffic is ambiguous free text today).

                Show the user what their session costs

                Challenge and why it costs

                Challenge. Your users cannot economise on a quantity they never see: to the person driving the agent, tokens are invisible until the monthly bill arrives, long after the behaviour that spent them.

                Why it costs. With no feedback signal, users have no reason to prefer the cheap phrasing over the expensive one, to reset a bloated session, or to notice that one workflow costs ten times another.

                Applies where the user bears or influences the cost: internal tools, developer assistants and shared platforms. For an end-customer-facing product, answer N/A on this lever; the control belongs in Agent Harness Guardrails and limits (per-caller limits).

                Assessment Answer each question for your workload, then open the guidance where you have a gap.
                Q1Does your interface show users what their session costs?
                How to close this gap best practice

                The short answer. Show a running figure in the interface, such as “this session has used about N tokens” or an approximate dollar amount. Users cannot economise on a quantity they never see.

                Read more for the self-serve reader

                Because you own the UX, you can surface the meter. A per-session indicator, such as "this session has used ~N tokens" or an approximate dollar figure, closes the feedback loop and changes behaviour. Mature coding assistants already do this, exposing session token usage and a locally computed cost figure to the developer (Anthropic, Manage costs effectively [19]).

                Q2Is that cost shown during the session, while users can still act?
                How to close this gap best practice

                The short answer. Show it live, during the session. An approximate number now changes behaviour; a precise number on next month’s invoice changes nothing.

                Read more for the self-serve reader

                Two properties matter more than precision. Timely: show it while the user can still act on it, during the session rather than on next month's invoice, because a signal that arrives after the spend changes nothing. Approximate is enough: the figure does not need to be billing-precise, and a locally computed estimate that may differ from the final bill still recruits the user into the cost loop.

                What it saves: Qualitative — recruits every user into the cost loop instead of leaving optimisation entirely to the platform team.

                  Each track is a separate assessment. Progress, applicable-answer coverage, notes, gaps, exports, printing and resets are calculated only from the track you open.

                  Use the two cards above to start or continue. There is deliberately no blended score across unlike operating models.

                  Start with the bill, because it is the one thing both tracks have in common. Figure 1 shows how it is calculated: you pay for the input tokens you send and for the output tokens the model returns, and the output rate is higher. Two levers move that total further than any others. Prompt caching reduces what you pay for input that repeats from one call to the next, and context hygiene reduces how much input you send in the first place. Every remaining lever in this runbook works on one of the two terms of that calculation: the input you are billed for, or the output.

                  Cost structure overview

                  Every agent is a model wrapped in a harness. The model sets the price of each token, and the harness determines how many tokens a task consumes. Both tracks therefore work through the same three layers, called actor-layers because each one has a different owner. At Model Inference, each call is priced. At Agent Harness, the loop multiplies the number of calls and the amount of context they carry. At End User, working habits determine how often that loop runs.

                  Each lever belongs in exactly one cell of the grid below: the track it applies to, and the layer where the decision to spend is actually taken. One cell means one owner, so no lever ends up half-owned by two people. The bill, though, is not divided that way. A task's cost is the three layers multiplied together: what each call costs, how many calls the loop makes, and how often someone runs it. So every lever has a clear owner, while the total has none, and none of the three owners can see it from where they sit. Bringing the total down takes all three of them, which is why the sections that follow cover all three layers rather than only your own.

                  Two levers sit just below the table. Reserved-tier commitments report 30 to 50 per cent at sustained volume, and model distillation reaches break-even typically 6 to 12 months past the cited thresholds. Both save materially, but both ask for a commitment or an upfront spend, so they belong after the audit rather than in the first week. Reserved also has a volume floor rather than only a commitment, so check your throughput clears the documented minimums before you plan around it (Match the pricing tier to the environment, Q2).

                  Pre-launch checklist

                  Run this before an agent, or a new team of assistant seats, sends its first real traffic. Each line is a section of this runbook compressed to a yes/no.

                  • Before first traffic
                  • Default model tier set deliberately, balanced default with a cheap background default, not whatever the framework shipped (Right-size the model to the task; Decision guidance: cost-aware model routing)
                  • Iteration cap, session token budget, and confidence exit enforced in harness code (Orchestration)
                  • Dev and test traffic on Flex tier, where the model and Region support it (Match the pricing tier to the environment)
                  • Hard spend cap at the request path, gateway or proxy, not an after-the-fact alert (Cost attribution and spending caps)
                  • Rate and concurrency ceilings set per team, not only monthly dollars (Cap concurrency in the code you own)
                  • Behind a gateway, all three consumption dimensions capped per caller, requests and inference tokens and concurrent connections, not request rate alone (Guardrails and limits)
                  • Attribution wired: application inference profiles tagged, budgets and anomaly detection on the tags (Attribute cost with application inference profiles)
                  • Cache verified with counters, per hop if a proxy chain is involved (Place and verify cache checkpoints; Verify the cache per hop in proxied chains)
                  • Invocation logging on, so background traffic is auditable from day one (Observability)
                  • Token-per-task and task-success baselines captured before launch (Know what you spend and what it buys)

                  Runtime signal quick scan

                  Runtime spend anomalies rarely announce themselves; these four signals catch them while they are still running.                   SignalTrack 1 checkTrack 2 checkPrinciple
                  Invocations nobody initiatedManage coding agent configurationsObservability
                  Parallel sessions multiplying spendCost attribution and spending capsCap concurrency in the code you own; Guardrails and limits
                  Healthy output hiding climbing spendManage the session and its context activelyMemoryUnchanged quality is not evidence of controlled cost

                  Cost-anomaly diagnostic checklist

                  The bill jumped and the workload did not. Work down this list; it is ordered by how often each cause is the answer and how fast it is to check.

                  1. Cache stopped landing. Read the CloudWatch CacheReadInputTokenCount metric; zero on a workload that should cache means a broken prefix or a proxy hop rewriting it (Verify the cache per hop in proxied chains). On an assistant fleet the usual cause is a developer rather than the pipeline: switching model or reasoning effort mid-session re-prefills the whole conversation, and so does returning after the cache has expired (Manage the session and its context actively).
                  2. A loop is not converging. Look for sessions or tasks with outlier round counts; context grows with the square of rounds (Agent loop token amplification; Orchestration).
                  3. Background or hidden invocations. Group invocation logs by caller and time of day; flat round-the-clock volume is not a human (Observability).
                  4. Retries multiplying spend. Check pass rates and orchestrator retry counts; a falling pass rate raises cost per successful task with no per-call change (Measure cost per successful task; Cost dimensions of the orchestration layer).
                  5. Sessions grew heavy under compaction. Cumulative session tokens against task complexity; quality will not warn you (Unchanged quality is not evidence of controlled cost).
                  6. A model moved under you. A pinned Legacy model on extended-access pricing, or a default that drifted to a dearer tier (Audit for Legacy / extended-access models; Right-size the model to the task).
                  7. Concurrency multiplied. More parallel sessions per developer than last month (Cap concurrency in the code you own).
                  8. Attribution is too coarse to say. If none of the above is checkable because the bill is one line item, the finding is the missing attribution itself (Attribute cost with application inference profiles).

                  Synthesis and next steps

                  The pattern holds across both tracks. At model selection and routing you right-size and, if you own the invocation, route to the cheapest model that clears the bar. At context and caching you cache the stable prefix and keep the working set lean so you stop re-billing tokens the task no longer needs. At invocation and output discipline you bound each call, on output length, quota burndown, and reasoning effort. At orchestration you push verbose work into subagents and, if you own the invocation, single-turn, no-tool generation work into batch, off the interactive path. At governance and attribution you set fleet defaults, hard caps, per-user attribution, and watch the model-lifecycle and seat clocks. The token meter all of that is measured against is the same on both tracks; the tracks differ only in which levers you actually hold. This is FinOps for AI, and it is the same discipline whether you build the agent or adopt one.

                  Next: an architecture track (LLM gateway, token-level attribution, budget enforcement) and an operating-model track will be covered in a subsequent issue. Claude Code-specific configuration for the agnostic practices above is deferred to the official Claude Code on Amazon Bedrock documentation [52].

                  Decision principles

                  Three rules in this runbook are literally identical whichever track you run: nothing about them changes with the operational surface, so they are covered once here rather than phrased twice and left to drift. Both tracks' navigation points at this block.

                  Compare models on cost per solved task, not price per token shared

                  The list price per token is the wrong axis for any model-tiering decision, because models differ in how many tokens, and how many attempts, they need to finish the same work. The comparison that decides the routing table is:

                  cost per solved task = total tokens billed across all attempts × price / successfully completed tasks

                  Measured this way, a pricier model can come out cheaper. A frontier model that answers in fewer output tokens, needs fewer correction rounds, and fails less often can undercut a nominally cheaper model whose per-task token volume and retry rate are higher. Output tokens are the expensive kind, so producing fewer of them moves the bill disproportionately. Practitioners comparing model tiers on identical tasks have reported exactly this inversion. So treat "smaller model = cheaper" as a hypothesis to test rather than a rule: run a representative task set through each candidate, count tokens billed and tasks solved, and let the ratio pick the model. The Know what you spend and what it buys lever keeps that comparison tied to a versioned cost and success baseline.

                  One further caution applies when the model arrives wrapped inside a packaged product rather than called directly. The same model name does not guarantee the same serving configuration. A wrapped deployment may differ from the direct API in context handling or output behaviour, in ways the product documentation does not cover. Where the comparison matters, cross-validate with the same benchmark task run through both paths before attributing a cost or quality difference to the model itself.

                  Unchanged quality is not evidence of controlled cost shared

                  Compaction and auto-summarisation are designed to preserve output quality as context grows, which means quality is the one signal that will not tell you the session has become expensive. A long session under automatic compaction keeps answering well while cumulative token spend climbs; the summarisation calls themselves bill, the retained context stays near the ceiling, and there is no visible degradation to prompt anyone to reset. The invoice becomes the first alarm, weeks late.

                  Watch a leading indicator instead: cumulative session token count against task complexity. A session whose token total keeps climbing while the task at hand is routine is the signature of context that compaction is preserving but the work no longer needs. The habit levers in Track 1 (Manage the session and its context actively) and the architecture levers in Track 2 (Memory) are the fixes; this signal is what tells you when to apply them.

                  Measure cost per successful task, not cost per call shared

                  Agents fail and retry, and a per-call or per-task cost figure that ignores failures understates real cost by the failure rate. An agent with a 70 per cent pass rate spends on 100 attempts to bank 70 results. Adjust for the pass rate:

                  cost per successful task = total spend across all attempts / successful outcomes

                  AWS calls the outcome-level metric cost-per-task-completion and recommends attributing planning, execution, reflection, verification, and tool costs to the workflow outcome (AWS Agentic AI Lens, AGENTCOST05-BP01 [105]).

                  For coding-agent workflows, Coding Agent Insights supplies token, latency, API, tool, approval, and organisational dimensions (Coding Agent Insights [74]; AWS OpenTelemetry setup for OpenAI Codex [104]). It does not know whether a coding task succeeded. Join telemetry to a defined successful outcome through a stable task or workflow key.

                  Track the result per workflow alongside the orchestration-to-execution ratio and the release-gate metrics in Know what you spend and what it buys. Use the same denominator for the cost-per-solved-task model comparison and coding-agent attribution.

                  Network, sandbox, approval, and tool-permission controls are governance and blast-radius containment. Their economic benefit is indirect unless local measurements show avoided incidents or rework. Do not report them as direct token savings.

                  Telemetry transport does not select or bill the inference provider. Codex bearer-token telemetry can send metrics to CloudWatch with any provider (AWS OpenTelemetry setup for OpenAI Codex [104]). When Codex uses Bedrock, Bedrock owns inference billing and AWS service support (OpenAI Codex on Amazon Bedrock [103]).
